modules.doc:
std.bytes — the raw byte view of a string: the honesty valve D25 buys
by refusing `s[i]` on `str`. Stability tier: core.

**This module had no code for five sprints, s37 gave it a producer, and
s81 closed the circle.** `str.bytes()` produces the byte view
(`List[byte]` since sc35 — one octet per element, and the TYPE says
0..255 now) on all three lanes, and `str_from_utf8` — the prelude's
validating way back, landed at s81
(wolf-lang#58, F-0057 CLOSED) — is what `to_str` delegates to. **All
nine reviewed functions are code now**; the module has no contract left.
`is_utf8` keeps its job, because the question "are these bytes text?"
has a boolean answer a caller may want without the text.

**`to_str` had unequal lanes for exactly one sprint, and it has three
now.** `str_from_utf8` is PURE (no I13 capability, no sandbox category —
the second such family after `json_*`) and executed on the compiler rungs
alone at sc13, where lupin 0.1.11 answered
`unsupported: `str_from_utf8` does not resolve` — the generic unknown-name
refusal rather than a reasoned decline, which is why it was filed as drift
(F-0075). **lupin 0.1.12 resolves it and the finding is CLOSED**,
re-measured with its own reproducer at the sc14 pin, so all nine functions
here are three-lane and the module has neither a contract nor an unequal
row left.

**THE ARGUMENT POSITION IS A LEND NOW, AND EIGHT OF THESE NINE
FUNCTIONS STOP COPYING** (s89, wolf-lang#86, F-0072 CLOSED — the ask
this header carried for two sprints, answered in the shape it asked
for). s77 made `s.bytes()` the receiver's own `{ptr, len}` wherever the
call was CONSUMED (`for b in s.bytes()`, `s.bytes().len`) and
materialized it everywhere else — including in an ARGUMENT, which is
how every function here receives its bytes, so `bytes.len(s.bytes())`
took a heap copy of `s` for a length it was going to read in place.
s89 is the region checker's argument one scale down: a view handed to a
callee is LENT for the call, the callee may read it, and it may not
outlive the call. So write `bytes.find(s.bytes(), needle)` and the view
crosses without a copy.

Three consequences worth knowing before writing against it.

- **The verdict is the CALLEE's, and it is decided from its body.** A
  parameter every one of whose uses is one of s77's read positions (or a
  re-lend into another lendable parameter) is lendable; anything the
  analysis has not proved materializes exactly as before, which is never
  wrong and only slower. Eight of the nine below are lendable and
  `to_str` is not: it hands its parameter to `str_from_utf8`, and a
  builtin consumer materializes. That is upstream's measurement
  (`wolf_mem`'s `byteview` suite, `a_builtin_consumer_materializes`),
  cited here rather than restated, because no lane in this repository
  can observe an allocation (§9's sc12 rule).
- **A lend that would outlive its call is REFUSED, not quietly copied**
  — `E1015`, with the one-word fix in the diagnostic: bind the bytes
  first (`let bs = s.bytes()` materializes) and the bound list is an
  ordinary value the callee may own. Nothing in this module trips it;
  the shape that would is a function returning its own `List[byte]`
  parameter.
- **`from_str` is the way IN and still allocates, which is its job.** A
  function that RETURNS a list must own it, so the copy is the price of
  having a VALUE rather than a walk — and a caller who only wants to walk
  should write `for b in s.bytes()` or call `std.str`'s walks, which do.
  The `Bytes` type this header has wanted since sc05 is still the thing
  that would make the interim currency real; the lend is what made the
  interim stop costing a copy per call.

What this module is FOR is unchanged and worth restating in that light:
bytes a program HOLDS (a decoder's output, a list it built, a buffer it
was handed) rather than bytes it is walking through once. A one-pass
walk over a string's bytes belongs in `std.str` and is written there.

**THE TYPE IS `List[byte]`, AND THE INTERIM IS OVER (sc35).** For nine
sprints this header carried a recorded interim — the currency was
`List[int]`, one element per byte, and the ELEMENT CONTRACT (0..255)
was a promise the library made and the type could not keep. Both
halves of the wait have landed. D72 / s135 gave the language
`[type.byte]` — an 8-bit unsigned octet whose `List[byte]` strides by
1 — and s136 (wolf-lang#231) moved the eight byte BUILTINS to it, which
is the half that decided whether this module could spend the type.
**So every signature below is the rename this header promised, and
nothing else moved**: `from_str` is still `s.bytes()`, `to_str` is
still `str_from_utf8(b)?`, and not one function here gained a
conversion loop.

**What the rename is worth, measured through THIS module's own
producers rather than synthetically** (F-0104's after-table, re-run at
the io sites — `docs/findings.md`): a 64 KiB buffer read by
`std.fs.read_bytes` charges **65,584 native and 65,536 checked**,
where the same read as `List[int]` charged 1,048,560 and 1,048,576.
**16.0x -> 1.00x native, 16.0x -> 1.00x checked.** The native number
is not the 2.0x sc34 predicted for a byte buffer, and the reason is
s136's: a PRODUCER mints its list at exact capacity through one
memcpy, so it pays no push-growth history at all — the 48 is one list
header. The 2.0x is still what a list this module GROWS by `push`
costs, and that residue is `[mem.region.account.1]`'s, not the
element width's.

**Three things about the element contract are now the TYPE's job and
not this module's.** A `List[byte]` cannot hold 300, cannot hold -1,
and cannot hold a non-byte — so `is_utf8`'s "an element outside 0..255
answers `false`" clause is unreachable rather than merely untested,
`to_str`'s matching row is too, and `hex.encode`'s §11 assert has one
fewer thing to defend. The clauses stay documented where the REASONING
is still worth having (a validator answers, an encoder traps) and are
marked unreachable where the type now forbids the input.

**The element is a `byte`, so reading one is a `byte` and widening is
SPELLED.** `at` returns `byte` — it is `b[i]`, and `b[i]` on a
`List[byte]` is an octet — so a caller comparing it to a number writes
`bytes.at(b, i) as int == 0x80` or `bytes.at(b, i) == 0x80 as byte`.
That is `[type.byte.op]`'s rule and not this module's opinion: `byte`
against `int` is the ordinary type mismatch, and every arithmetic
operator widens to `int` anyway. Comparing two bytes needs no cast at
all, which is why `find`, `starts_with` and `ends_with` did not change
a line of their bodies.

**Why these five duplicate `std.list`'s names, and why that is right.**
`len`, `is_empty`, `at`, `find`, `starts_with` and `ends_with` all have
`std.list` counterparts, and the reason to have both is measured rather
than aesthetic: `std.list`'s are GENERIC, and a generic std function
runs on the interpreter lane alone (both compiler rungs refuse
monomorphization at a module boundary, F-0026), while these are
monomorphic over `List[byte]` and run on all three. A program that has
bytes wants the byte-tier operations to be available wherever it
compiles. The vocabulary is §8's, deliberately: one concept, one name,
across all of std — `len`, `is_empty`, `find`, `starts_with`,
`ends_with`, `slice`, `at`.

**What byte-land buys, in one line each.** `ends_with` is trivial here
and needed the boundary primitive over `str`; `slice` can never split a
code point because there are no code points here; `at` is legal
indexing where `s[i]` is refused for `str` (D25 licenses exactly this).
The freedom has a price, and it is the whole reason `to_str` validates:
bytes are where the UTF-8 invariant is ALLOWED to be absent.

**The border post, and why it took five sprints — kept because the
reason is the design.** `to_str` was a reviewed contract from sc05 to
sc12 and the blocker was never tables: nothing in the language built a
`str` from a number (no `char`, no `from_utf8`, no `strbuf.push_byte`,
probed four ways at four pins), so the MATERIALIZATION step had nowhere
to happen while the VALIDATION half sat here written and tested as
`is_utf8`. An ASCII-only `to_str` would have been a border post that
refuses text, which §9 forbids, so the function waited.

What it waited for is exactly what landed. s77 made the byte view
bit-identical to a `str` and deliberately emitted no path back, naming
the reason in the compiler's own words — the view "cannot become a
`str` … a `List[int] -> str` conversion would have to VALIDATE
(wolf-std's `bytes.to_str`, still blocked, and this is why: it wants a
checked primitive, not a cast)". s81 wrote that primitive: a `{utf8}`
row rather than a trap, a cast nowhere in it, and the same six
rejection classes `is_utf8` enumerates plus one this library could not
have raised at all (an element that is not a byte). std did not lower
its standard and the toolchain did not take the shortcut; the border
post is the same function the sc05 contract described, four lines long.

items.name: at
items.sig: fn at(b: prelude.List[byte], i: int) -> byte · regions (ρ1, -) -> -
items.doc:
The byte at index `i`. **BYTE INDEXING IS LEGAL HERE** — it is the
whole point of this type (D25 licenses `b[i]` exactly where it refuses
`s[i]`), and this function is the spelling that does not presume the
answer to F-0011's builtin-versus-std question.

Traps `bounds` when `i` is out of range — the language's own fault from
the language's own indexing, because a caller that could have checked
`len` and did not has violated a contract (§8). The recoverable
spelling is `std.list.get`, which raises `none`.

```wolf-doc-example
bytes.at("hé".bytes(), 0) as int == 104
bytes.at("hé".bytes(), 1) as int == 195
bytes.at("hé".bytes(), 2) == 169 as byte
```
items.summary: The byte at index `i`.

doctests.code:
bytes.at("hé".bytes(), 0) as int == 104
bytes.at("hé".bytes(), 1) as int == 195
bytes.at("hé".bytes(), 2) == 169 as byte

items.name: ends_with
items.sig: fn ends_with(b: prelude.List[byte], suffix: prelude.List[byte]) -> bool · regions (ρ1, ρ2) -> -
items.doc:
Whether `b` ends with `suffix`; the empty suffix always does. Total: no
error row, no traps.

Note what byte-land buys: this one is three lines here and needed the
boundary primitive to exist at all over `str`, where the tail offset
may fall inside a code point.

```wolf-doc-example
bytes.ends_with("wolf".bytes(), "lf".bytes()) == true
bytes.ends_with("wolf".bytes(), "wo".bytes()) == false
bytes.ends_with("wolf".bytes(), "".bytes()) == true
```
items.summary: Whether `b` ends with `suffix`; the empty suffix always does.

doctests.code:
bytes.ends_with("wolf".bytes(), "lf".bytes()) == true
bytes.ends_with("wolf".bytes(), "wo".bytes()) == false
bytes.ends_with("wolf".bytes(), "".bytes()) == true

items.name: find
items.sig: fn find(b: prelude.List[byte], needle: prelude.List[byte]) -> int ! {none} · regions (ρ1, ρ2) -> -
items.doc:
The index of the first occurrence of `needle` in `b`; `none` when it
does not occur. The empty needle occurs at 0, exactly as `str.find`'s
does. A needle longer than `b` is a miss, not a fault. Total otherwise:
no traps.

```wolf-doc-example
(bytes.find("wolf".bytes(), "lf".bytes()) else 0 - 1) == 2
(bytes.find("wolf".bytes(), "z".bytes()) else 0 - 1) == 0 - 1
(bytes.find("wolf".bytes(), "".bytes()) else 0 - 1) == 0
```
items.summary: The index of the first occurrence of `needle` in `b`; `none` when it does not occur.

doctests.code:
(bytes.find("wolf".bytes(), "lf".bytes()) else 0 - 1) == 2
(bytes.find("wolf".bytes(), "z".bytes()) else 0 - 1) == 0 - 1

items.name: from_str
items.sig: fn from_str(s: str) -> prelude.List[byte] · regions (-) -> ρ_caller
items.doc:
`s`'s bytes — infallible, because a valid `str` is always valid bytes.
The bare-noun/`as_`-grade direction of §1 (a view, not a conversion of
meaning). It is no longer the only producer: `std.fs.read_bytes` and
`std.fs.read_chunk` hand back bytes that were never a `str` (s90,
F-0044 closed), which is the case this module's element contract was
always written for. `str.bytes(s)` is the same view from the other
side.

**This function materializes, and after s77 that is a statement about
its SIGNATURE rather than about the pin.** The language's `s.bytes()` is
the receiver's own pointer and length when it is consumed on the spot;
returning it — which is all this function does — is one of the positions
that still copies, and it must be, because the list outlives the
expression that produced it. So the allocation is the price of having a
value rather than a walk, and a caller who only wants to walk should
write `for b in s.bytes()` (or call `std.str`'s walks, which do). Total:
no error row, no traps beyond allocation.

**Call it when you want to KEEP the bytes, not to pass them.** Since s89
an argument is a lend, so `bytes.len(s.bytes())` is the spelling that
hands the eight lendable functions below the string's own two words,
while `bytes.len(bytes.from_str(s))` allocates a list in order to throw
it away. Reach for this function when the list outlives the call: a
buffer a program accumulates into, a decoder's output, anything held
across statements — which is what the doc examples below still do
wherever a value is what the reader needs to see.

```wolf-doc-example
bytes.at(bytes.from_str("A"), 0) as int == 65
bytes.len(bytes.from_str("🐺")) == 4
bytes.at(bytes.from_str("🐺"), 0) as int == 240
```
items.summary: `s`'s bytes — infallible, because a valid `str` is always valid bytes.

doctests.code:
bytes.at(bytes.from_str("A"), 0) as int == 65
bytes.len(bytes.from_str("🐺")) == 4
bytes.at(bytes.from_str("🐺"), 0) as int == 240

items.name: is_empty
items.sig: fn is_empty(b: prelude.List[byte]) -> bool · regions (ρ1) -> -
items.doc:
Whether `b` holds no bytes. Total: no error row, no traps.

```wolf-doc-example
bytes.is_empty("".bytes()) == true
bytes.is_empty("x".bytes()) == false
```
items.summary: Whether `b` holds no bytes.

doctests.code:
bytes.is_empty("".bytes()) == true
bytes.is_empty("x".bytes()) == false

items.name: is_utf8
items.sig: fn is_utf8(b: prelude.List[byte]) -> bool · regions (ρ1) -> -
items.doc:
Whether `b` is well-formed UTF-8 — the predicate half of `to_str`, and
the one function here that reads the bytes as text rather than as
numbers. The empty sequence is valid.

It stays hand-written now that `to_str` exists, and the reason has
OUTLIVED the reason it was written for. It was kept at sc13 because it
had three lanes where `to_str` had two (F-0075, since closed), and that
argument is spent; what is not spent is the other one: two independent
decoders that must agree are worth more than one. The agreement is a
test (`tests/bytes/to_str_border.lu`) rather than a tautology, and it is
the test that would catch either side drifting — this module's RFC 3629
reading or the toolchain's.

It rejects everything the standard rejects, not merely truncation: a
stray continuation byte, a truncated multi-byte sequence, an OVERLONG
form (`C0 80` for U+0000, `E0 80 80`, `F0 80 80 80`), a surrogate
(U+D800..U+DFFF, `ED A0 80`), a scalar above U+10FFFF (`F4 90 80 80`),
and the bytes `C0`, `C1`, `F5`..`FF` which begin no sequence at all.

**An element outside 0..255 makes it `false`, not a trap.** §11 has
element-range violations trap `assert`, and that rule is an ENCODER's:
`hex.encode` must not render a number it was not given. A validator is
the opposite case — the question "are these bytes text?" has an answer
for a non-byte, the answer is no, and a predicate that traps is a
predicate every caller must guard before calling, which defeats it.

Total: no error row, no traps.

```wolf-doc-example
bytes.is_utf8("héllo 🐺".bytes()) == true
bytes.is_utf8("".bytes()) == true
var bad = List[byte]()
(mut bad).push(255 as byte)
bytes.is_utf8(bad) == false
```
items.summary: Whether `b` is well-formed UTF-8 — the predicate half of `to_str`, and the one function here that reads the bytes as text rather than as numbers.

doctests.code:
bytes.is_utf8("héllo 🐺".bytes()) == true
bytes.is_utf8("".bytes()) == true
var bad = List[byte]()
(mut bad).push(255 as byte)
bytes.is_utf8(bad) == false

items.name: len
items.sig: fn len(b: prelude.List[byte]) -> int · regions (ρ1) -> -
items.doc:
The number of bytes in `b`. O(1). Total: no error row, no traps.

```wolf-doc-example
bytes.len("wolf".bytes()) == 4
bytes.len("é".bytes()) == 2
bytes.len("".bytes()) == 0
```
items.summary: The number of bytes in `b`.

doctests.code:
bytes.len("wolf".bytes()) == 4
bytes.len("é".bytes()) == 2
bytes.len("".bytes()) == 0

items.name: slice
items.sig: fn slice(b: prelude.List[byte], from: int, to: int) -> prelude.List[byte] · regions (ρ1, -, -) -> ρ_caller
items.doc:
The bytes in `[from, to)`, as a fresh list. Never splits a code point,
because there are no code points here — the freedom this view sells.

Traps `assert` when the range is out of order (`to < from`), starts
below zero, or ends past `len(b)`. **This is a recorded delta from the
reviewed contract**, which said `bounds`: with `List[byte]` as the
interim currency there is no slice SYNTAX to inherit the language's
fault from, so the check is std's own and the kind is the one std can
raise (§2 — either way it is a caller contract violation, and either
way the process ends). It becomes `bounds` when `Bytes` lands with a
slicing form.

```wolf-doc-example
bytes.len(bytes.slice("wolf".bytes(), 1, 3)) == 2
bytes.at(bytes.slice("wolf".bytes(), 1, 3), 0) as int == 111
bytes.len(bytes.slice("wolf".bytes(), 2, 2)) == 0
bytes.len(bytes.slice("wolf".bytes(), 0, 4)) == 4
```
items.summary: The bytes in `[from, to)`, as a fresh list.

doctests.code:
bytes.len(bytes.slice("wolf".bytes(), 1, 3)) == 2
bytes.at(bytes.slice("wolf".bytes(), 1, 3), 0) as int == 111
bytes.len(bytes.slice("wolf".bytes(), 2, 2)) == 0
bytes.len(bytes.slice("wolf".bytes(), 0, 4)) == 4

items.sig: fn starts_with(b: prelude.List[byte], prefix: prelude.List[byte]) -> bool · regions (ρ1, ρ2) -> -
items.doc:

no error row, no traps.

```wolf-doc-example
bytes.starts_with("wolf".bytes(), "wo".bytes()) == true
bytes.starts_with("wolf".bytes(), "lf".bytes()) == false
bytes.starts_with("wolf".bytes(), "".bytes()) == true
```
items.summary: Whether `b` begins with `prefix`; the empty prefix always does.

doctests.code:
bytes.starts_with("wolf".bytes(), "wo".bytes()) == true
bytes.starts_with("wolf".bytes(), "lf".bytes()) == false

items.name: to_str
items.sig: fn to_str(b: prelude.List[byte]) -> str ! {utf8} · regions (ρ1) -> -
items.doc:
`b` as text, VALIDATED — the border post D24 demands, the one place in
wolf where bytes become a `str`, and the reason `str` needs no validity
check anywhere else.

Rows: `utf8`, and nothing else. **Nothing here traps**, including for
input this module's own element contract calls impossible: a stray
continuation byte, a truncated sequence, an overlong form, a surrogate
(U+D800..U+DFFF), a scalar above U+10FFFF, a byte that begins no
sequence (`C0`, `C1`, `F5`..`FF`), and an element outside 0..255 are all
a MISS. Bytes are data — §2's rule, and the same reasoning that makes
`is_utf8` answer `false` rather than trapping on a non-byte.

An interior NUL is VALID and is not a terminator: a wolf `str` carries
its length, so `to_str` of `[119, 0, 102]` is a three-byte string.

`is_utf8` is this function's predicate half and the two agree by
measurement, not by construction — they are different code (one is a
decoder written here in divisions and range tests, the other is the
toolchain's), and `tests/bytes/to_str_border.lu` walks the classes
through both and asserts they answer the same. Ask `is_utf8` for a
boolean; call `to_str` when you want the text.

Pure: `str_from_utf8` carries no I13 capability and no sandbox
category, so with `json_*` it is the second such builtin family and
the D33 sandbox has no reason to refuse it. That is a statement about
the SANDBOX and not a promise about comptime, because the engine
cannot reach this function for an unrelated reason: `List[byte]()`
inside a `comptime fn` is `unsupported` at resolve (F-0077), and a
`List` is the only way to spell the argument. Measured, both compiler
rungs, rather than inferred from the absence of a capability.

Delegates to the prelude's `str_from_utf8` (s81, wolf-lang#58). **Three
lanes** as of the sc14 pins: both compiler rungs had it at s81 and lupin
0.1.12 resolves it too (F-0075, filed at sc13 and closed one release
later), so this function's test columns are all lit and no caller pays a
lane for reading text out of bytes.

```wolf-doc-example
(bytes.to_str(bytes.from_str("wolf é")) else "?") == "wolf é"
(bytes.to_str(List[byte]()) else "?") == ""
var lone = List[byte]()
(mut lone).push(128 as byte)
(bytes.to_str(lone) else "?") == "?"
```
items.summary: `b` as text, VALIDATED — the border post D24 demands, the one place in wolf where bytes become a `str`, and the reason `str` needs no validity check anywhere else.

doctests.code:
(bytes.to_str(bytes.from_str("wolf é")) else "?") == "wolf é"
(bytes.to_str(List[byte]()) else "?") == ""
var lone = List[byte]()
(mut lone).push(128 as byte)
(bytes.to_str(lone) else "?") == "?"

modules.doc:
std.cmp — comparison and ordering: the `Ordering` enum, the `Eq` and
`Ord` protocols, and the min/max/clamp family. Stability tier: core.

Decided here and recorded (sc01): f64 ordering. Its `Ord` is
`total_cmp` (IEEE totalOrder), so sorting floats is legal and NaN
has one home (above `+inf`). See `total_cmp` for the two documented
approximations at the current pins.

**`f64` HAS AN `Eq` NOW, AND sc44 REVERSED sc01 TO GIVE IT ONE.**
This header said for forty-three sprints that `f64` has no `Eq`
because "IEEE partial comparison stays on the builtin operators".
`[type.trait.op]` (s155, wolf-lang#5) is what retires that sentence:
since the operator bridge landed, `==` on a type parameter IS
`Eq.eq`, so "stays on the builtin operator" and "goes through `Eq`"
stopped being two different places. Withholding the impl would not
have kept a partial order out of a total protocol; it would only
have made `f64` the one primitive whose `==` does not work under a
bound, while `<` under the same bound did. The impl's body is
`self == other` — the clause's rule that a primitive impl IS the
builtin operation — and the law caveat is stated on the impl
itself: reflexivity fails at NaN, which is exactly what the builtin
does and is why `Ord for f64` is `total_cmp` and not this.

INTERIM SPELLINGS (each filed, flipped on the pin bump that fixes it):
- The absence-spelling interim is RETIRED (F-0003, dead at the sc05
  pins, renamed tree-wide at sc06): a lowercase bare tag resolves in
  every implementation. Until sc12 this line still described the
  interim, in a half-renamed sentence that said the source said the
  opposite of what it says.
- `Ord` requires `Eq` by doctrine, and the requirement is still
  DOCUMENTARY, but for a smaller reason than it was. s155 gave the
  grammar a `trait_item` with an `=` form (the alias bound,
  `[type.trait.op.alias]`) and no supertrait clause, so composition
  this edition is an alias listing both and not `trait Ord: Eq`.
  F-0004's operator half is RULED — `==`, `!=` and the relationals
  dispatch through `Eq`/`Ord` by name on a type parameter or a user
  type, which is what `std.ops` is written against — and its
  supertrait half is what remains open.
- **F-0006 IS RETIRED AND `impl Ord for str` SHIPS.** The finding
  said "wolfc rejects `<` on `str` (E0409) and one rejected body
  poisons every test that imports this module". Re-measured at the
  sc44 pins on all three lanes: `cmp.Ord.cmp("a", "b").is_lt()` is
  `true` on the checked tier, the body passes the static ladder on
  every lane, and nothing is poisoned. The impl is written here in
  the same shape as `Ord for int` — two relational tests and a
  fallthrough — and the order it reports is the language's
  byte-lexicographic one (`[mem.str.order]`), which `std.sort`'s
  `sort_strs` already documents is not alphabetical in any human
  language (F-0019 owns collation).
modules.summary: std.cmp — comparison and ordering: the `Ordering` enum, the `Eq` and `Ord` protocols, and the min/max/clamp family.

items.name: clamp
items.sig: fn clamp[T: self.Ord](v: T, lo: T, hi: T) -> T · regions (ρ1, ρ2, ρ3) -> ρ_caller
items.doc:
`v` limited to `[lo, hi]`: `lo` when `v < lo`, `hi` when `v > hi`,
else `v`. Traps `assert` when `lo > hi` — a contract violation the
callee cannot repair (`[conf.trap.map]`: user assertions).
items.summary: `v` limited to `[lo, hi]`: `lo` when `v < lo`, `hi` when `v > hi`, else `v`.

items.sig: fn max[T: self.Ord](a: T, b: T) -> T · regions (ρ1, ρ2) -> ρ_caller

items.name: total_cmp
items.sig: fn total_cmp(a: f64, b: f64) -> self.Ordering · regions (-, -) -> ρ_caller
items.doc:
IEEE totalOrder over floats, monomorphic: -inf < negative reals <
-0.0 < +0.0 < positive reals < +inf < NaN. Total: no error row, no
traps (f64 division by zero is IEEE, not a trap — X3 governs
integers).

Two documented approximations at the current pins (no f64 bit
intrinsics exist to do better): NaN is one value — the sign and
payload of a NaN are not observed, so every NaN sorts above `+inf`
and all NaNs compare `Equal`; totalOrder's -NaN-below--inf home is
not represented.

**Back in the fence at sc47, verbatim, as sc44 promised.** These
four lines were a `wolf-doc-example` from sc01 to sc43, went to
prose at sc44 when `==` between two `Ordering`s became
`fail(E0301)` on both compiler rungs (the operator trait resolved
by BARE name, and an importer of this module has only `cmp.Eq`),
and wolf-lang#336 closed that in v0.2.12. Measured here at
0.2.12/0.1.34: all four lines, all three lanes, `exit(0)`.

Each line is `true`: `total_cmp(1.0, 2.0)` agrees with
`total_cmp(-1.0e9, 3.5)` (both `Less`), `total_cmp(2.0, 1.0)` with
`total_cmp(0.0 / 0.0, 1.0)` (both `Greater` — NaN above every real),
`total_cmp(4.5, 4.5)` with `total_cmp(0.0 / 0.0, 0.0 / 0.0)` (both
`Equal` — all NaNs are one value here), and `total_cmp(-0.0, 0.0)`
with `total_cmp(1.0, 2.0)` (both `Less` — the sign of zero is
observed).

```wolf-doc-example
cmp.total_cmp(1.0, 2.0) == cmp.total_cmp(-1.0e9, 3.5)
cmp.total_cmp(2.0, 1.0) == cmp.total_cmp(0.0 / 0.0, 1.0)
cmp.total_cmp(4.5, 4.5) == cmp.total_cmp(0.0 / 0.0, 0.0 / 0.0)
cmp.total_cmp(-0.0, 0.0) == cmp.total_cmp(1.0, 2.0)
```
items.summary: IEEE totalOrder over floats, monomorphic: -inf < negative reals < -0.0 < +0.0 < positive reals < +inf < NaN.

doctests.code:

cmp.total_cmp(2.0, 1.0) == cmp.total_cmp(0.0 / 0.0, 1.0)
cmp.total_cmp(4.5, 4.5) == cmp.total_cmp(0.0 / 0.0, 0.0 / 0.0)
cmp.total_cmp(-0.0, 0.0) == cmp.total_cmp(1.0, 2.0)

modules.doc:
std.fs — the filesystem, over rows: whole texts and whole BYTES, a
file-descriptor tier for the streaming cases, directories, metadata,
and pure path arithmetic. Stability tier: core.

**Errors are rows, never traps** (D30, and API-CONVENTIONS §2's
trap rule): a missing file, a refused permission, a host failure and
a text that is not UTF-8 are all ORDINARY outcomes a caller handles
with `else` or propagates with `?`. Nothing in this module traps, and
nothing returns a sentinel. The vocabulary is the builtin tier's,
adopted verbatim so that std adds no translation layer — s38's five,
and s90's three:

- `not_found` — the path does not exist (or, on a write, its parent
  directory does not)
- `denied` — the host refused the operation for permission reasons
- `io` — every other host failure, coarsened to one tag because no
  caller can act differently on them yet (§12's rule 3)
- `utf8` — the bytes are not well-formed UTF-8; wolf `str` is UTF-8
  by definition, so a text read that cannot decode is a miss. The
  BYTE tier below has no `utf8` row anywhere, which is its point.
- `eof` — a read reached the end of the file, which is an outcome
  rather than a failure (the fd tier only)
- `exists` — the path is already there and the operation demanded to
  create it (`create_dir`, and nothing else here)
- `invalid` — DECLARED AND UNREACHABLE FROM TYPED CODE since sc35.
  It named a `List[int]` element that is not a byte (outside 0..255)
  offered to a byte write — the WRITE's spelling of the refusal
  `str_from_utf8` makes on the way in (writing is not decoding, so
  `utf8` would be a lie). The byte writes take `List[byte]` now, so
  no typed caller can build the argument that raises it; the tag
  stays in the vocabulary because §14 says the vocabulary is the
  toolchain's and an FFI caller's wrong-width list still earns it
  (wolf-lang#231's own posture, adopted verbatim)
- `cross_device` — declared by `fs_rename` and never raised by this
  module: `move_file` HANDLES it, which is what the fallback below is
  for

**Capability: `fs` (I13).** Every function here reaches the host
filesystem, is tagged `fs` in the toolchain's sandbox table, and is
categorically refused at comptime (D33) — a `comptime fn` cannot read
a file, and the refusal names the reason. s90 widened the surface and
did NOT widen the sandbox: the fifteen new builtins carry the same tag
and the same categorical refusal. The pure path helpers at the bottom
of this module are the exception in both directions: they touch
nothing and are comptime-safe.

**The three-way split** (§8/§9's rule, applied to files). The
IMPLEMENTATION owns the builtins this module delegates to — s38's
nine (`fs_read_text`, `fs_write_text`, `fs_open`, `fs_create`,
`fs_read`, `fs_write`, `fs_close`, `fs_remove`, `fs_exists`) and
s90's fifteen (`fs_open_mode`, `fs_read_bytes`, `fs_write_bytes`,
`fs_read_chunk`, `fs_write_chunk`, `fs_read_dir`, `fs_create_dir`,
`fs_create_dir_all`, `fs_remove_dir`, `fs_remove_dir_all`,
`fs_rename`, `fs_is_file`, `fs_is_dir`, `fs_size`,
`fs_modified_ms`), s142's `fs_fstat`, and s199's three
(`fs_seek`, `fs_tell`, `fs_read_at` — wolf-lang#426, with the
standard streams as handles 0, 1 and 2, #424) — so their semantics
are part of this module's contract and are documented per
function. std owns everything else:
the `File` value, the consuming `close`, the mode choice behind
`append_text`/`open_append`, `move_file`'s fast path and its
fallback, and the path arithmetic. The LANGUAGE owns nothing here;
there is no file syntax.

**Paths are `str`, forward slashes travel everywhere.** wolf has no
`Path` type at v0 and this module does not invent one: a path is a
`str` the host interprets. Write forward slashes in wolf literals on
every platform — windows accepts them at the API, and a backslash in a
wolf literal is an ESCAPE (`"C:\Users"` does not lex, seven times over
in the s38 test sweep). The path helpers here therefore split on `/`
only, and say so.

**THE WORKAROUNDS ARE GONE, AND WHAT REPLACED THEM IS WORTH NAMING**
(s90, wolf-lang#51/#52, F-0044 and F-0045 both CLOSED). For seven
sprints three of this module's functions were shaped by builtins that
did not exist, and their docs said so:

- `append_text` read the whole file, concatenated in memory and wrote
  it back, behind an `fs_exists` check its own doc called a race. It
  is `fs_open_mode(path, 2)` + one write + one close now: it touches
  no existing byte, it asks no question whose answer can change under
  it, and its `utf8` row went with the read that no longer happens.
- `copy_file` and `move_file` were TEXT operations, so a file holding
  a lone `0x80` did not survive them. Both are byte operations now,
  and both lost `utf8` for the same reason.
- `move_file` was copy-then-remove as its ONLY path. `fs_rename` is
  the fast path now and copy-then-remove is the FALLBACK, reached
  through the `cross_device` row the builtin declares for exactly
  this purpose.

**What is still deliberately absent**, each a reviewed contract
rather than an approximation:

- `rename(from, to)` as an ATOMIC move — **WITHDRAWN, not blocked.**
  The contract asked for atomicity; the language deliberately does
  not promise it, because POSIX `rename(2)` replaces a destination
  atomically and windows `MoveFileEx` is documented to replace but
  not to replace atomically. Upstream therefore ships `fs_rename`
  claiming only the EFFECT and no `fs_rename_atomic` at all, per the
  platform rule (a promise that cannot be kept on a tier-1 target
  does not get a `#[cfg]` that keeps it on two out of three). std
  adopts that reading rather than re-promising it one level up:
  `move_file` is the wrapper, it says what it does and does not
  guarantee, and there is no second name for the same call. The one
  atomically-promisable primitive the language DOES offer everywhere
  is `fs_open_mode`'s create-new mode, which nothing in std needs
  yet; the sprint that writes a lock file or a unique temp name
  wraps it, and this paragraph is where that decision was recorded.
- `stem` / `extension` — a pair that has to decide what a dot means
  (a leading dot, a doubled extension, no dot at all). That was never
  a filing about the builtin tier; it is a design question this
  module has not answered, and the earlier citation of F-0044 beside
  it was wrong.
- `is_absolute`, and `join`'s behaviour on an absolute `name` —
  documented on `join` itself.
- `io.Read`/`io.Write` traits and buffering — blocked on trait
  dispatch (F-0004), not on the filesystem. Every write here is
  unbuffered and every function says so.

**What this module CANNOT witness, stated rather than implied**
(§14's rule for a claim a green rig would otherwise imply):
`denied` needs a permission call, `cross_device` needs two
filesystems, and `read_dir`'s `utf8` needs a file name the host holds
in bytes no `str` can carry. None of the three has a portable litmus,
so no test here observes them; their meanings are documented on the
functions and nothing claims more. `move_file`'s fallback is reached
only through `cross_device`, so the TRIGGER is unwitnessed here even
though the fallback's body — `copy_file` then `remove` — is two
tested functions.

**Lanes (re-measured at the sc12 pin, one call at a time).** BOTH
compiler rungs are executing lanes: the checked tier performs real
host operations and the native rung lowers all twenty-four fs
builtins over the eu ABI (s90, `RT_SYMBOLS` 83 -> 94), so every new
function here lands with two lanes from its first commit rather than
gaining the second one later. The comptime sandbox is the one place
these operations are refused (D33). lupin has no fs builtins by
design, and the refusal for the s90 names is the generic
unknown-name one (``unsupported: `fs_read_dir` does not resolve``,
measured) rather than a reasoned decline — but lupin resolves module
bodies LAZILY, so the pure path helpers RUN there:
modules.summary: std.fs — the filesystem, over rows: whole texts and whole BYTES, a file-descriptor tier for the streaming cases, directories, metadata, and pure path arithmetic.

items.name: append_text
items.sig: fn append_text(path: str, text: str) -> () ! {IoErrors}
items.doc:
Append `text` to the end of the file at `path`, creating it when it
is absent.

Rows: `not_found` when the parent directory does not exist, `denied`
when the host refuses, `io` for any other host failure. Never traps.

**It is an append now, and the three things that used to be true
about it are not.** Until s90 there was no append-mode open, so this
function read the whole file, concatenated in memory and wrote it
back — behind an `fs_exists` check that was a check-then-use race its
own doc had to warn about. It opens the file in append mode, writes
once and closes:

- it reads NO existing byte, so its cost is in `text` rather than in
  the file's size, and a `utf8` row is gone with the decode that no
  longer happens — appending to a file that is not valid UTF-8 is now
  an ordinary append;
- it asks no question whose answer can change before it acts: the
  create and the open are one host call, so the absent-file case
  needs no probe;
- every write lands at the end of the file AS IT IS AT THE MOMENT OF
  THE WRITE (the mode's whole point), so two processes appending
  lines to one log no longer lose one of them.

What it still does not promise: that ONE call is atomic. A single
short write to an append handle is what the host makes of it, and
nothing in the language claims more.

The handle is closed on every exit, including the error path, by a
`defer` — which is the idiom §12 records for exactly this and the
reason a failed write here does not leak a descriptor.

Capability `fs`; refused at comptime (D33). Delegates to
`fs_open_mode` (mode 2), `fs_write` and `fs_close`.

```wolf-doc-example
fs.write_text("doc-append.tmp", "one\n")?
fs.append_text("doc-append.tmp", "two\n")?
(fs.read_text("doc-append.tmp") else "?") == "one\ntwo\n"
fs.remove("doc-append.tmp")?
```
items.summary: Append `text` to the end of the file at `path`, creating it when it is absent.

doctests.code:
fs.write_text("doc-append.tmp", "one\n")?
fs.append_text("doc-append.tmp", "two\n")?
(fs.read_text("doc-append.tmp") else "?") == "one\ntwo\n"
fs.remove("doc-append.tmp")?

items.name: close
items.sig: fn close(take f: self.File) -> () ! {io} · regions (ρ1) -> -
items.doc:
Close `f`, consuming it.

Rows: `io` when the handle was already closed or is foreign. Never
traps.

`take` is the mode of the operation's meaning (§3: `take` only where
the value is genuinely gone afterwards): closing ends the handle's
life, so the caller spells `fs.close(take f)` and the compiler
rejects every later use of `f` as a use-after-move. That is the whole
staleness story for files, and it costs nothing at run time.

A closed descriptor is never reused by the builtin tier at this pin,
so a forged or stale `File` answers `io` rather than reaching another
caller's file. Do not depend on that beyond this pin: the mode system
is the guarantee, the table's behaviour is an implementation detail.

Capability `fs`; refused at comptime (D33). Delegates to `fs_close`.

```wolf-doc-example
var f = fs.create("doc-close.tmp")?
fs.close(take f)?
fs.remove("doc-close.tmp")?
```
items.summary: Close `f`, consuming it.

doctests.code:
var f = fs.create("doc-close.tmp")?
fs.close(take f)?
fs.remove("doc-close.tmp")?

items.name: copy_file
items.sig: fn copy_file(from: str, to: str) -> () ! {IoErrors}
items.doc:
Copy the BYTES of `from` to `to`, replacing `to` if it exists.

Rows: `not_found` when `from` does not exist or `to`'s parent
directory does not, `denied` when the host refuses either half, `io`
for any other host failure. Never traps.

**It is a byte copy now, and the row it lost says so.** Until s90 it
was `read_text` + `write_text`, which meant a file holding a lone
`0x80` came back refused with `utf8` — a copy that works on text and
corrupts (or declines) everything else. It is `fs_read_bytes` +
`fs_write_bytes`, there is no decode anywhere in it, and `utf8` is
gone from the row because nothing here can raise it.

`fs_write_bytes` declares `invalid` for an element that is not a
byte. This function cannot raise it: the bytes came out of
`fs_read_bytes` one line earlier and are bytes by construction. The
handler below therefore reports `io` on that arm — the coarsening a
caller could not act on differently — rather than widening this
signature with a tag no input can reach (§14: a function's row is the
union of what its delegates raise, MINUS what it handles itself).

Not atomic, and it reads the whole file into memory: a file larger
than the process wants to hold wants the fd tier's `read_chunk` /
`write_chunk` in a loop. Copying a file onto itself truncates it and
is not a supported operation.

Capability `fs`; refused at comptime (D33).

```wolf-doc-example
fs.write_text("doc-copy-src.tmp", "wolves\n")?
fs.copy_file("doc-copy-src.tmp", "doc-copy-dst.tmp")?
(fs.read_text("doc-copy-dst.tmp") else "?") == "wolves\n"
fs.remove("doc-copy-src.tmp")?
fs.remove("doc-copy-dst.tmp")?
```
items.summary: Copy the BYTES of `from` to `to`, replacing `to` if it exists.

items.name: create
items.sig: fn create(path: str) -> self.File ! {denied, io} · regions (-) -> ρ_caller
items.doc:
Create (or truncate) the file at `path` for WRITING and return its
handle.

Rows: `denied` when the host refuses, `io` for any other host failure
— including a parent directory that does not exist, which the builtin
tier does not distinguish here the way `write_text` does. Never traps.

An existing file is truncated to nothing, which is the operation's
point: `create` is how a program writes a file it means to own. The
handle must be closed with `close`, which consumes it.

Capability `fs`; refused at comptime (D33). Delegates to `fs_create`.

```wolf-doc-example
var f = fs.create("doc-create.tmp")?
fs.write(mut f, "pack")?
fs.close(take f)?
(fs.read_text("doc-create.tmp") else "?") == "pack"
fs.remove("doc-create.tmp")?
```
items.summary: Create (or truncate) the file at `path` for WRITING and return its handle.

items.name: create_dir
items.sig: fn create_dir(path: str) -> () ! {denied, exists, io, not_found}
items.doc:
Create ONE directory at `path`.

Rows: `exists` when something is already there — a directory, a file,
anything — because this function's contract is that it CREATED the
directory, and "it was already here" is a different outcome a caller
may well act on. `not_found` when the parent directory does not
exist: this form creates exactly one level. `denied` when the host
refuses, `io` for any other host failure. Never traps.

`create_dir_all` is the idempotent form: it creates the parents and
an existing directory is not an error there, which is what makes it
the one to reach for before a write. Reach for THIS one when the
creation is the point — a lock directory, a run whose output must not
land on top of an earlier one.

Capability `fs`; refused at comptime (D33). Delegates to
`fs_create_dir`.

```wolf-doc-example
fs.create_dir("doc-create-dir.tmp")?
fs.is_dir("doc-create-dir.tmp") == true
var again = false
fs.create_dir("doc-create-dir.tmp") else |_| { again = true }
again == true
fs.remove_dir("doc-create-dir.tmp")?
```
items.summary: Create ONE directory at `path`.

doctests.code:
fs.create_dir("doc-create-dir.tmp")?
fs.is_dir("doc-create-dir.tmp") == true
var again = false
fs.create_dir("doc-create-dir.tmp") else |_| { again = true }
again == true
fs.remove_dir("doc-create-dir.tmp")?

items.name: create_dir_all
items.sig: fn create_dir_all(path: str) -> () ! {denied, io}
items.doc:
Create the directory at `path` and every missing parent of it.

Rows: `denied` when the host refuses, `io` for any other host
failure — which includes a path whose parent is a regular FILE, since
no directory can be created under it. Never traps.

**It is idempotent, and that is why it has no `exists` row**: a
directory that is already there is success, because the caller asked
for the directory to EXIST rather than for it to be created. There is
no `not_found` either — a missing parent is the thing this function
makes.

Capability `fs`; refused at comptime (D33). Delegates to
`fs_create_dir_all`.

```wolf-doc-example
fs.create_dir_all("doc-create-all.tmp/a/b")?
fs.is_dir("doc-create-all.tmp/a/b") == true
fs.create_dir_all("doc-create-all.tmp/a/b")?
fs.remove_dir_all("doc-create-all.tmp")?
```
items.summary: Create the directory at `path` and every missing parent of it.

doctests.code:
fs.create_dir_all("doc-create-all.tmp/a/b")?
fs.is_dir("doc-create-all.tmp/a/b") == true
fs.create_dir_all("doc-create-all.tmp/a/b")?
fs.remove_dir_all("doc-create-all.tmp")?

items.name: create_dir_mode
items.sig: fn create_dir_mode(path: str, mode: int) -> () ! {denied, exists, invalid, io, not_found, unsupported}
items.doc:
`create_dir`, with the directory's permission bits: `mode` less the
process's umask.

`[os.fs.create.mode]`. One level, as `create_dir`; `mkdir -m` is this
call and then `set_mode`, since `-m` is not subject to the umask.

Rows: `invalid` when `mode` is outside `0..=0o777`; `exists`,
`not_found`, `denied`; `unsupported` on a host with no permission
bits; `io` otherwise. Never traps.

Capability `fs`; refused at comptime (D33). Delegates to
`fs_create_dir_mode`.

```wolf-doc-example
var row = "ok"
fs.create_dir_mode("doc-dir-mode.tmp", 0o1000) else |_| { row = "refused" }
row == "refused" && !fs.exists("doc-dir-mode.tmp")
```
items.summary: `create_dir`, with the directory's permission bits: `mode` less the process's umask.

items.name: create_private
items.sig: fn create_private(path: str) -> self.File ! {denied, exists, io, not_found, unsupported} · regions (-) -> ρ_caller
items.doc:
Create a NEW file at `path` that only its owner can read or write,
open for reading and writing.

`[os.fs.create.mode]` (wolf-lang#346, wolf-std#5): one exclusive
create with mode `0o600`, so the file is never readable by anyone
else, not even for the instant between a `create` and a `set_mode` —
the shape a key, a token or a temporary file wants. It never reuses a
file that is already there.

Rows: `exists` when anything is at `path`; `not_found` when the
parent directory is missing; `denied` when the host refuses;
`unsupported` on a host with no permission bits (windows, by name: a
private file there is an access-control list, which this call does
not pretend to write); `io` otherwise. Never traps.

Capability `fs`; refused at comptime (D33). Delegates to
`fs_open_perm`.

```wolf-doc-example
var made = true
var f = fs.create_private("doc-create-private.tmp") else |_| {
    made = false
    fs.create("doc-create-private.tmp")?
}
fs.close(take f)?
let info = fs.stat("doc-create-private.tmp")?
fs.remove("doc-create-private.tmp")?
!made || info.mode == 0o600
```
items.summary: Create a NEW file at `path` that only its owner can read or write, open for reading and writing.

    fs.create("doc-create-private.tmp")?
}
fs.close(take f)?

fs.remove("doc-create-private.tmp")?

items.name: fstat
items.sig: fn fstat(mut f: self.File) -> self.Stat ! {IoErrors} · regions (ρ1) -> ρ_caller
items.doc:
One metadata read on the open handle `f`.

`[os.fs.fstat]`. This is `fs.size` and `fs.modified_ms` and
`fs.is_dir` and `fs.is_file`, answered together, off the handle a
program is about to read anyway — one host call instead of four path
resolutions.

**The reason is a measurement, not a tidiness.** wolf-lang#261: a
static-file server was paying four path stats per request
(`is_dir`, `is_file`, `size`, `modified_ms`) where nginx pays one
`open` and one `fstat`, and the last two could not move into the
program because nothing in this module answered off a handle. Now
something does, and the four path calls stay exactly where they are
for the callers that have a path and no handle.

Rows are the path stat's, so one handler serves both spellings:
`not_found`, `denied`, `io`. On a HANDLE the hosts answer `io` for
nearly everything — the entry is already resolved, so the misses the
path calls have are behind it — and a closed or forged handle is
`io`, this family's rule. A size or a time outside `int` is `io`,
`fs.size`'s rule. Never traps.

**The one host difference is `fs.open`'s, and it is stated.** linux,
macOS and freebsd open a directory read-only, so a `File` over a
directory exists there and `kind` **1** is reachable. **Windows
refuses to open a directory as a file — `fs.open` answers `denied`,
not this call** — so on windows every handle this function ever sees
is a file or a device, `kind` 1 never appears, and a server that
classifies directories does it BY PATH with `fs.is_dir`, as it did
before this call existed. That is a difference in what can be
OPENED, not in what `fstat` reports, and no row here moves with the
host.

`mut f` because a metadata read is a host call on the handle, and
§14's stream rule has the call site spell it. The handle's read
position is not disturbed.

Capability `fs`; refused at comptime (D33). Delegates to `fs_fstat`
(s142) — both compiler lanes. The clause says every tier-1 host on
every tier serves it, "the checked machine reads the same handle
metadata the runtime does", and lupin still answers `unsupported`:
the REFERENCE machine has no filesystem at all by design, so the
whole fs tier is declined there rather than mocked, and that is a
posture and not a release date. It is the one place a zero pairing
gap buys this module nothing.

```wolf-doc-example
var f = fs.open("doc-fstat.tmp")?
let st = fs.fstat(mut f)?
fs.close(take f)?
fs.remove("doc-fstat.tmp")?
st.kind == 0 && st.size == 6 && st.modified_ms > 0
```

helper that hides a bug (the day `is_absolute` exists, this doc says

is the shape every directory walk takes.

second name of the link. The call never replaces, which makes it the

`existing` or `path`'s parent is missing; `cross_device` across two

items.name: modified_ms
items.sig: fn modified_ms(path: str) -> int ! {IoErrors}
items.doc:
When the file at `path` was last modified, in MILLISECONDS from the
Unix epoch — negative before it.

Rows: `not_found` when the path does not exist, `denied` when the
host refuses, `io` for any other host failure, which includes a host
that has a file but no modification time for it. Never traps.

**The unit is in the name, and that is a departure this doc owes an
explanation.** §14's rule is that when a builtin hands std a bare
`int` whose UNIT is the whole contract, std names the unit in a TYPE
— which is why `std.time` ships `Instant` and `Duration`. Returning a
`time.Instant` here would make `std.fs` depend on `std.time`, and a
dependency between two std modules is charged per PROGRAM at this pin
(two modules that declare a same-named function cannot be linked into
one native binary, F-0026), so every program that touched a file
would carry the calendar. The unit therefore rides in the name, where
it is at least impossible to miss. The scale is deliberately
`time_unix_ms`'s, so `time.unix_ms() - fs.modified_ms(p)?` is an age
in milliseconds with no conversion — and the day a `Path`/`Instant`
pair is worth the dependency, that is the signature change to make.

Resolution is the host's: a filesystem that stores seconds answers
multiples of 1000, and nothing here rounds or pretends otherwise.

`fs_modified_ms`.

```wolf-doc-example
stamp > 0
(fs.modified_ms("doc-modified-absent.tmp") else 0 - 1) == 0 - 1
fs.remove("doc-modified.tmp")?
```

items.name: move_file
items.sig: fn move_file(from: str, to: str) -> () ! {IoErrors}
items.doc:
Move the file at `from` to `to`.

Rows: `not_found` when `from` does not exist or `to`'s parent
directory does not, `denied` when the host refuses, `io` for any
other host failure. Never traps.

**The host rename is the fast path and copy-then-remove is the
fallback** — which is the other way round from every earlier pin,
where the copy was the only path. The rename moves the directory
entry without reading a byte, so a gigabyte within one filesystem
costs the same as an empty file. Two of `fs_rename`'s rows are the
fallback's triggers rather than failures, and this function handles
both:

- `cross_device` — `from` and `to` are on different filesystems
  (`EXDEV`, `ERROR_NOT_SAME_DEVICE`), which no rename can do
  anywhere. The fallback is `copy_file` then `remove`, and because
  `copy_file` is a BYTE copy the fallback is a real fallback and not
  a text operation wearing a disguise.
- `exists` — the destination is there and this host's rename will not
  replace it. unix replaces a file and an empty directory; windows
  refuses a directory outright. The fallback replaces it, so callers
  see one behaviour on every tier-1 target instead of the platform's.

**It is not atomic and it does not claim to be.** A host rename is
atomic within a filesystem on unix; windows does not promise that,
so the LANGUAGE does not promise it (there is no `fs_rename_atomic`)
and neither does this function. On the fallback path it is plainly
not atomic: a failure between the copy and the remove leaves both
files, which is the same exposure this function has always had and is
now the uncommon case rather than the only one.

The fallback's TRIGGER cannot be witnessed portably — a test would
need two filesystems — so no test here reaches it, and the module
header says so. Its body is `copy_file` followed by `remove`, both of
which are tested.

Capability `fs`; refused at comptime (D33). Delegates to `fs_rename`,
and to `copy_file` + `fs_remove` on the fallback.

the end. `unseekable` for a handle with no position. Never traps.

with `std.bytes.to_str` — where the validation happens once, over the

and the bytes a second call sees depend on the first.

items.name: read_dir
items.sig: fn read_dir(path: str) -> prelude.List[str] ! {denied, io, not_found, utf8} · regions (-) -> ρ_caller
items.doc:
The entry NAMES directly inside the directory at `path`, SORTED.

Rows: `not_found` when the path does not exist, `denied` when the
host refuses, `io` for any other host failure — which includes
asking a regular file for its entries. `utf8` when an entry's name is
bytes no `str` can carry: the LISTING fails rather than the entry
being dropped, because a `read_dir` that silently omits a file lies
about the directory. Never traps.

**Names, not paths.** An entry comes back as `"today.txt"`, never as
`"logs/today.txt"` — join it yourself with `join`, which is the pure
helper at the bottom of this module and exists for exactly this.
Returning names is the builtin's decision and std does not decorate
it: a caller who wants paths says so in one call, and a caller who
wants names cannot get them back out of a path without cutting.

**Sorted is a promise, and it is the toolchain's.** Filesystem order
differs per filesystem, so an unsorted listing makes every program
written against it machine-dependent and every test of one a coin
flip. The order is by the name's bytes, which is `str`'s own
relational order (`[mem.str.order]`) and therefore the order
`std.sort` would put them in. `.` and `..` are not entries and do not
appear.

The listing is a snapshot, not a lock: an entry can be gone by the
time the caller opens it, which is the same check-then-use caveat
`exists` carries.

`fs_read_dir`.

```wolf-doc-example
names.len == 2
names[0] == "alpha.txt"
names[1] == "beta.txt"
fs.remove_dir_all("doc-read-dir.tmp")?
```

set-group-id and sticky — written in octal, `0o640`; the umask plays
no part. A final symbolic link is FOLLOWED: the call changes what
the link names, never the link.

Rows: `invalid` when `mode` is outside `0..=0o7777`, decided before
the host is asked; `not_found` when nothing is at `path` (a dangling
link included); `denied` when this process does not own the file;
`unsupported` on a host with no permission bits (windows, by name);
`io` otherwise. Never traps.

`fs_set_mode`.

let info = fs.stat("doc-set-mode.tmp")?
fs.remove("doc-set-mode.tmp")?
(row == "ok" && info.mode == 0o600) || (row == "refused" && !fs.answered(info, 4))

items.name: set_owner
items.sig: fn set_owner(path: str, uid: int, gid: int) -> () ! {denied, invalid, io, not_found, unsupported}
items.doc:
Set the owner and the group of what is at `path`, following a final
symbolic link — `chown`.

`[os.fs.owner]` (wolf-lang#701): one host call. `uid` and `gid` are
the ids `stat` answers (`Info.uid`, `Info.gid`), or `owner_keep()` to
leave one as it is — so `chgrp` is `set_owner(p, fs.owner_keep(),
gid)`. **Who may** is the host's rule: the super-user may set any
owner; anyone else may move a file they own to a group they are in,
and may not give a file away. **The host clears the set-user-id and
set-group-id bits** when an owner changes, so a program that wants
them sets the owner first and the mode after (`set_mode`) — `cp -p`'s
order.

Rows: `invalid` when an id is neither `owner_keep()` nor in
`0..=4294967294` (decided before the host), or is one the host has
no mapping for; `denied` when this process may not make the change;
`not_found` (a dangling link included); `unsupported` on a host with
no owners (windows, by name); `io` otherwise. Never traps.

Capability `fs`; refused at comptime (D33). Delegates to
`fs_set_owner`.

```wolf-doc-example
var refused = false
fs.set_owner("doc-set-owner.tmp", 0 - 2, fs.owner_keep()) else |_| { refused = true }
refused == true
```
items.summary: Set the owner and the group of what is at `path`, following a final symbolic link — `chown`.

items.name: set_times
items.sig: fn set_times(path: str, atime: self.Time, mtime: self.Time) -> () ! {denied, invalid, io, not_found} · regions (-, ρ1, ρ2) -> -
items.doc:
Set the access time and the modification time of what is at `path`,
following a final symbolic link.

`[os.fs.times]` (wolf-lang#700): one host call. Each of `atime` and
`mtime` is a `time(s, ns)`, `time_now()` or `time_keep()`, so one
call sets both, sets one and keeps the other, or stamps now —
`touch`, `touch -a`, `touch -m`, and the last step of `cp -p`. A
file system keeps the precision it has (windows 100 ns steps; some
keep seconds): compare what `stat` reads back, not what was asked.

Rows: `invalid` when a `Time`'s `ns` is neither a count below one
second nor one of the two special values; `not_found`; `denied`;
`io` otherwise. Never traps.

Capability `fs`; refused at comptime (D33). Delegates to
`fs_set_times`.

```wolf-doc-example
fs.write_text("doc-set-times.tmp", "x")?
fs.set_times("doc-set-times.tmp", fs.time_keep(), fs.time(1500000000, 0))?
let info = fs.stat("doc-set-times.tmp")?
fs.remove("doc-set-times.tmp")?
info.mtime_s == 1500000000 && info.modified_ms == 1500000000000
```

items.name: size
items.sig: fn size(path: str) -> int ! {IoErrors}
items.doc:
The size of the file at `path`, in BYTES.

Rows: `not_found` when the path does not exist, `denied` when the
host refuses, `io` for any other host failure. Never traps.

Bytes are the currency here as they are in `std.str` (§9): this is
the number `read_bytes` will hand back, and for a text file it is the
number `read_text`'s result reports as `len`. The size of a DIRECTORY
is whatever the host says it is and means nothing portable; ask
`read_dir` how many entries there are instead.

A size read is not a lease. The file can grow between this call and
the read that follows it, which is why nothing in this module sizes a
file in order to read it.

items.sig: fn stderr() -> self.File · regions () -> ρ_caller
items.doc:
The process's standard error, as a `File` — `stdin`'s doc in every
respect, for descriptor 2. `write` and `write_chunk` through it put
bytes on standard error; `std.io.write_err` stays the writer for text.

items.name: stdin
items.sig: fn stdin() -> self.File · regions () -> ρ_caller
items.doc:
The process's standard input, as a `File`.

`[os.fs.std]` (wolf-lang#424): the handle numbers 0, 1 and 2 are the
three streams the process was started with, and no open ever answers
one of them. This is that number in this module's type, so the
handle calls below can ask what standard input IS — a regular file
(`fstat(mut f)?.kind == 0`, and then its size), a pipe or a terminal
(`kind` 2) — and, when it is a file, read it at an offset without
reading forward to get there.

**What it serves:** `fstat`, `seek`, `seek_by`, `seek_end`, `tell`
and `read_at` (wolf 0.2.22, s199), and, from wolf 0.2.26 (s200,
wolf-lang#405), the BYTES: `read`, `read_chunk`, `write` and
`write_chunk` serve 0, 1 and 2 as the descriptors themselves
(`[os.fs.std]`). A read of 0 starts at the offset this process
shares with whoever started it and moves it; a pipe, socket or
terminal is read as what it is, and `eof` at its end. A write to 1
or 2 lands in program order with `print` and `std.io`'s writers,
unbuffered by this module. A closed standard stream is `io` (the
host's `EBADF`), never a silent success. **What it does not:**
`close` answers `io` on it, as on any handle no open made — nothing
here closes a standard stream, and there is no way to.
`tests/fs/std_bytes_rows.lu` writes 1 between two `print`s and reads
0 to its end.

Total, and reaches nothing until a call is made on the value.
Capability `fs` for the calls that take it.

The example runs with descriptor 1 a pipe — the rig's — and a pipe
has no position, so the seek is refused (`unseekable`, by name;
`tests/fs/std_handles.lu` asserts the tag):

```wolf-doc-example
var o = fs.stdout()
let at = fs.seek(mut o, 0) else 0 - 7
at == 0 - 7
```
items.summary: The process's standard input, as a `File`.

items.doc:
The process's standard output, as a `File` — `stdin`'s doc in every

bytes on standard output in program order with `print` (wolf 0.2.26,
`[os.fs.std]`); `std.io.write` stays the writer for text.

items.name: symlink
items.sig: fn symlink(target: str, path: str) -> () ! {denied, exists, invalid, io, not_found, unsupported}
items.doc:
Make `path` a symbolic link whose target is `target`, stored
verbatim.

`[os.fs.symlink]` (wolf-lang#698): `ln -s target path`. The target
is not resolved, not checked and not made absolute — `read_link`
reads the same bytes back — so a relative target means what the host
makes it mean when the link is followed, and a link to nothing is
made like any other.

Rows: `invalid` when `target` is empty; `exists` when anything is
already at `path` (the call never replaces); `not_found` when the
parent directory is missing; `denied`; `unsupported` on a host
without unprivileged symbolic links (windows, by name); `io`
otherwise. Never traps.

Capability `fs`; refused at comptime (D33). Delegates to
`fs_symlink`.

```wolf-doc-example

fs.symlink("", "doc-symlink.tmp") else |_| { row = "refused" }
row == "refused" && !fs.exists("doc-symlink.tmp")
```
items.summary: Make `path` a symbolic link whose target is `target`, stored verbatim.

items.name: tell
items.sig: fn tell(mut f: self.File) -> int ! {io, unseekable} · regions (ρ1) -> -
items.doc:
`f`'s position, from the start of the file, without moving it.

`[os.fs.tell]` (wolf-lang#426). A handle fresh from `open` answers 0;
after reads of `a` and `b` bytes it answers `a + b`. Rows:
`unseekable` for a handle with no position, `io` for a closed or
forged handle or a host failure. Never traps.

`mut f` for the stream rule (§14): the call site spells that the
handle is in play, as `fstat` does.

Capability `fs`; refused at comptime (D33). Delegates to `fs_tell`.

```wolf-doc-example

var f = fs.open("doc-tell.tmp")?

head.len == 4
(fs.tell(mut f) else 0) == 4
fs.close(take f)?
fs.remove("doc-tell.tmp")?
```

`[os.fs.truncate]` (wolf-lang#702): shorter, the tail gone; or
longer, the new bytes zeros no write stored. The handle's position
does NOT move, so a write after a truncation lands where the last
one ended.

Rows: `invalid` when `len` is negative; `io` for every host refusal
— a handle not open for writing, a directory, a pipe — and for a
closed or forged handle. Never traps.

`fs_truncate`.

```wolf-doc-example

fs.write(mut f, "0123456789")?
fs.truncate(mut f, 4)?
fs.close(take f)?
let size = fs.size("doc-truncate.tmp")?
fs.remove("doc-truncate.tmp")?
size == 4
```

items.name: write
items.sig: fn write(mut f: self.File, text: str) -> () ! {io} · regions (ρ1, -) -> -
items.doc:
Write `text` to `f` at its current position, advancing it.

Rows: `io` when the handle is closed, foreign or read-only, or the
host failed. Never traps, and there is no `utf8` row: a `str` is
already well-formed UTF-8.

`mut f` for the same reason `read` takes it: the position advances.
Writes are unbuffered — every call reaches the host — so a program
that writes small pieces in a loop pays for each one, and the
buffered writer that would fix it waits on trait dispatch (F-0004).

On a handle from `open_append` the position is the END of the file at
the moment of each write, so "current position" means what the mode
says rather than what an earlier write left behind.

Capability `fs`; refused at comptime (D33). Delegates to `fs_write`.

```wolf-doc-example
var f = fs.create("doc-write.tmp")?
fs.write(mut f, "one ")?
fs.write(mut f, "two")?
fs.close(take f)?
(fs.read_text("doc-write.tmp") else "?") == "one two"
```

items.name: write_bytes
items.sig: fn write_bytes(path: str, b: prelude.List[byte]) -> () ! {denied, invalid, io, not_found} · regions (-, ρ1) -> -
items.doc:
Write `b` to `path` as bytes, replacing whatever was there and
creating the file if it does not exist.

Rows: `not_found` when the path's parent directory does not exist,
`denied` when the host refuses, `io` for any other host failure, and
**`invalid` — declared and UNREACHABLE from typed code (sc35).** It
named an element of `b` that is not a byte (outside 0..255), which
the interim `List[int]` currency (§11) made spellable; `b` is a
`List[byte]` now and cannot hold one. Never traps.

The tag is not removed, and that is deliberate: §14 says the row
vocabulary is the toolchain's, `fs_write_bytes` still declares
`invalid` (wolf-lang#231 kept it on purpose — an FFI caller's
wrong-width list still earns it), and dropping a tag a caller may
have written a handler for is a breaking change this rename is not.
The witness moved with the contract: `tests/fs/invalid_row.lu` is a
static E0401 rejection now.

The row was a deliberate departure from §11's encoder rule, which
has `hex.encode` TRAP on an element out of range — and at sc35 both
halves of that disagreement are moot, because neither door can be
reached. The reasoning is kept because it is still the rule for the
next row: a library that traps where the toolchain raises has taken
a decision away from its caller.

Not atomic, exactly as `write_text` is not.

Capability `fs`; refused at comptime (D33). Delegates to
`fs_write_bytes`.

```wolf-doc-example
var raw = List[byte]()
(mut raw).push(119 as byte)
(mut raw).push(0 as byte)
(mut raw).push(102 as byte)
fs.write_bytes("doc-write-bytes.tmp", raw)?
(fs.size("doc-write-bytes.tmp") else 0 - 1) == 3
fs.remove("doc-write-bytes.tmp")?
```

```wolf-doc-example
fs.close(take f)?
```

rather than atomicity (see its doc, and the module header on why the

items.name: File
items.sig: struct File { fd: int }
items.doc:
An open file: the host descriptor this process may read from or
write to, according to how it was opened.

The field is an `int` because that is what the builtin tier hands
out — a small non-negative index into the machine's file table, never
a pointer, and never reused after `close` at this pin. Reading it is
legal and occasionally useful in a diagnostic; passing a hand-built
`File` to `read` or `write` is not a trap but a miss (`io`), because a
forged descriptor is a checkable condition rather than a contract
violation.

**Staleness is prevented by the mode system, not by a generation
counter.** `close` takes its `File` by `take` (X1), so a caller that
closes a file and then reads it is rejected statically as a
use-after-move — the discipline a generational handle would enforce
dynamically, enforced earlier and for free. `std.pool`'s handles need
generations because a pool hands out many; a `File` has exactly one
owner.

The value does not record which MODE opened it. Writing to a handle
`open` produced is `io`, and reading one `create` produced is `io`,
because the host refuses — not because this struct checked.
items.summary: An open file: the host descriptor this process may read from or write to, according to how it was opened.

items.name: Info
items.sig: struct Info { kind: int, size: int, modified_ms: int, have: int, mode: int, nlink: int, uid: int, gid: int, blocks: int, dev: int, ino: int, rdev: int, atime_s: int, atime_ns: int, mtime_s: int, mtime_ns: int, ctime_s: int, ctime_ns: int, btime_s: int, btime_ns: int }
items.doc:
The full stat record of one path: what `ls -l` shows.

`[os.fs.stat]` (wolf-lang#625, #536). Twenty host words, named. The
first three are `Stat`'s, in its units — `kind`, `size` in bytes,
`modified_ms` from the Unix epoch — and `kind` is finer here: **0**
regular file, **1** directory, **2** anything the host does not name,
**3** symbolic link, **4** fifo, **5** socket, **6** character device,
**7** block device.

`have` says which words the host ANSWERED: bit `i` for word `i` of
the clause's table (0 kind, 1 size, 2 modified_ms, 3 have, 4 mode,
5 nlink, 6 uid, 7 gid, 8 blocks, 9 dev, 10 ino, 11 rdev, 12–13 atime,
14–15 mtime, 16–17 ctime, 18–19 btime). A word whose bit is clear is
0 and is the host's refusal, by name — windows answers no `mode`,
`nlink`, owner, `blocks`, identity or `ctime`; linux answers a birth
time only where the filesystem keeps one. `answered(info, word)` reads
the bit.

`mode` is the permission bits with set-user-id, set-group-id and
sticky (`0o7777`), the file type being `kind`. `blocks` is in 512-byte
units. `dev` and `ino` are the file's identity: two paths name one
file when both agree — compare them, never order them. A time is a
`timespec`: whole seconds from the epoch (negative before it) and
nanoseconds in `0..999999999`.

**A new type, not a wider `Stat`**: `Stat`'s three fields are built by
literal in programs that already exist, and a wider struct would
refuse every one of them.
items.summary: The full stat record of one path: what `ls -l` shows.

items.name: Stat
items.sig: struct Stat { kind: int, size: int, modified_ms: int }
items.doc:
What one metadata read on an open handle answers: a kind, a size and
a modification time.

**A typed value rather than the `[kind, size, modified_ms]` triple
the builtin hands over.** `fs_fstat` answers a `List[int]`, and a
caller reading `got[0]`, `got[1]`, `got[2]` is a caller who has to
remember an ORDER — §14's rule is that when a builtin hands std a
positional row whose meaning is the contract, std names the positions
in a type. `stat.size` cannot be confused with `stat.modified_ms`;
`got[1]` and `got[2]` can be, and silently.

`kind` is **0** for a regular file, **1** for a directory, **2** for
anything else — a fifo, a socket, a device. It is an `int` and not an
enum because `std` has no closed-enum vocabulary at this pin and a
three-constant enum invented here would be a shape no other module
shares; the numbers are the clause's own (`[os.fs.fstat]`) and the
predicates below are what a program actually calls.

`size` is bytes, `fs.size`'s word in `fs.size`'s units.
`modified_ms` is milliseconds from the Unix epoch, negative before
it — `fs.modified_ms`'s word in its units, deliberately, so the
handle's answer and the path's compare with no conversion. The unit
rides in the field name for exactly the reason it rides in
`modified_ms`'s function name, and that doc carries the argument.
items.summary: What one metadata read on an open handle answers: a kind, a size and a modification time.

items.name: Time
items.sig: struct Time { s: int, ns: int }
items.doc:
One time `set_times` writes: a moment, "now", or "leave it".

`[os.fs.times]`. `s` is whole seconds from the Unix epoch (negative
before it) and `ns` nanoseconds in `0..999999999` — `Info`'s
`mtime_s`/`mtime_ns`, so what `stat` read can be written back — or
`ns` is one of the clause's two special values, which `time_now` and
`time_keep` build so that no caller writes the numbers.
items.summary: One time `set_times` writes: a moment, "now", or "leave it".

modules.doc:
std.list — the documented API surface of the language's `List[T]`:
the growable sequence every other module hands back. Stability tier:
core.

**What is the language's and what is std's** (sc02's structural
finding, F-0011): `List[T]` is a language-blessed core type — both
implementations provide it natively, the spec owns its semantics, and
the three operations below stay the language's own:

- construction: `List[T]()`;
- indexing: `xs[i]` reads, and an out-of-range index traps `bounds`
  in every profile (X3 posture) — every function here that names an
  index inherits exactly that trap;
- iteration: `for x in xs`.

Everything else — this file — is std's. Functions take the container
as their first parameter with an honest X1 mode: `mut` where mutation
IS the operation, the bare `read` default everywhere else.

Two operations joined the language's list at the sc44 pins and they
are worth naming because a learner reaches for them first: SLICING
(`xs[..n]`, `xs[1..]`, `[mem.list.slice]`) runs on all three lanes
now, and it is the language's, not std's. There is no
`list.prefix`/`list.suffix` and there will not be one — §8 forbids a
std name that shadows a working builtin — and there cannot be a
`list.take` either, because `take` is a reserved word (`E0008` on
both machines: the ownership verb owns it).

**THE METHOD SPELLINGS ARE NOT STD'S TO GIVE (wolf-std#25).** A
learner coming from chapter 5 writes `(mut l).truncate(2)` or
`l.remove(i)` and gets "wolf cannot compile this yet — methods on
generic std data" from the compiler and "`List` has no method
`truncate` in this machine's std subset" from lupin. Both refusals
are about the LANGUAGE's method surface on the builtin `List`, and
std cannot extend it: this module is free functions over a container,
by §8's rule, and `list.truncate(mut l, 2)` is the spelling it
offers. All three of `insert`, `remove` and `truncate` are here, with
bodies, with fenced doc examples that execute, and with three-lane
ledger rows (`list/insert_remove.lu`, `list/clear_truncate_fill.lu`)
— so the gap the issue found is a gap in what a learner is TOLD, not
in what std ships. None of the three is written over the slice: the
bodies rebuild through the private `at`, which predates slicing by
nine sprints and stays because it is correct, and a rewrite would be
churn against three green rows.

Regions (D10): every function allocates in the ambient region and no
signature asks for one. The `.in(r)` targets are s37's plumbing, not
this module's. **s76 made that sentence true of the machine and not
only of the API** (the sc12 pin): a `List` allocates in the ambient
region AT THE SITE, so a list built inside `region r { }` is freed with
it and growth stays in the region it was born in. Nothing here changed
to earn that, which is the point — a region-silent algorithm inherits
its operands' homes, and now it does so in fact rather than in
intention.

HISTORY, kept because two campaigns of bodies were shaped by it:
- **The single-read rule is DEAD** (s72's D40, `[mem.iter.excl]`, closed
  at the sc11 pin). wolfc's mem tier used to treat every read of a
  container place as a MOVE, so two read SITES over one binding in one
  body was E1001 (`xs.len` twice; `xs.len` then `xs[i]`; `for x in xs`
  then anything), and that is why every body here reads through `len`
  and the private `at` — one call per site — instead of projecting
  twice. Iteration takes a read claim over the loop's whole extent now,
  `for` no longer moves its iterable, and a write during the loop is
  `E1013` statically and `trap(exclusivity)` dynamically (F-0005 and
  F-0014, both closed). The bodies keep their shape because they are
  correct and rewriting them would be churn; new code in this module
  does not need the ceremony.
- The absence-spelling interim is retired: the tag is lowercase
  everywhere as of sc06 (F-0003 dead), and this header carried a
  half-renamed sentence about it — "`none`, not the convention's
  `none`" — for six sprints afterwards. A rename that touches 148 sites
  should have a reader on the prose too.

INTERIM SPELLINGS (each filed, flipped by the pin bump that fixes it):
- The `[T: Eq]` family (`contains`, `index_of`, `last_index_of`,
  `dedup`, `starts_with`, `ends_with`) is NOT in this file: importing
  std.cmp for the bound would make every importer of std.list
  `unsupported` under wolfc's checked tier (its trait/enum items are
  not executable there — F-0012), on top of trait dispatch running
  nowhere (F-0002/F-0004). The six sit in `std/x/list_eq/` with their
  bodies, and the stub comment below is their home here.
modules.summary: std.list — the documented API surface of the language's `List[T]`: the growable sequence every other module hands back.

items.doc:

items.name: clear
items.sig: fn clear[T](mut xs: prelude.List[T]) · regions (ρ1) -> -
items.doc:
Empties `xs`, keeping it usable. Total: no error row, no traps.
D10 note: the elements' storage belongs to the region, so clearing
drops no elements one by one for POD element types.

```wolf-doc-example
var xs = List[int]()
list.push(mut xs, 1)
list.clear(mut xs)
list.is_empty(xs) == true
```
items.summary: Empties `xs`, keeping it usable.

doctests.code:

list.push(mut xs, 1)
list.clear(mut xs)

items.name: concat
items.sig: fn concat[T](a: prelude.List[T], b: prelude.List[T]) -> prelude.List[T] · regions (ρ1, ρ2) -> ρ_caller
items.doc:
A new list holding `a`'s elements followed by `b`'s; both operands
are read, not consumed (`to_`-style allocation, §1). Total: no error
row, no traps beyond allocation.

```wolf-doc-example
var a = List[int]()
var b = List[int]()
list.push(mut a, 1)
list.push(mut b, 2)
list.len(list.concat(a, b)) == 2
```
items.summary: A new list holding `a`'s elements followed by `b`'s; both operands are read, not consumed (`to_`-style allocation, §1).

items.name: count_where
items.sig: fn count_where[T](xs: prelude.List[T], pred: fn(T) -> bool) -> int · regions (ρ1, -) -> -
items.doc:
How many elements satisfy `pred`. The whole walk, always — there is
nothing to stop early for.
items.summary: How many elements satisfy `pred`.

items.name: enumerate
items.sig: fn enumerate[T](xs: prelude.List[T]) -> prelude.List[(int, T)] · regions (ρ1) -> ρ_caller
items.doc:
A new list pairing each element of `xs` with its index, in order:
`(0, x0), (1, x1), …`. The shape `for (i, x) in list.enumerate(xs)`
destructures. Total: no error row, no traps beyond allocation.

`[type.comb.set]` (wolf-lang `4c046f15`): the method `xs.enumerate()`
is this call. Cost, as the clause states it: one fresh `List` of
pairs, indices from 0, plus `push`'s own copy of each pair — the
pairs escape with the element inside them
(`[mem.tier0.mode.read]`, wolf-lang#366), and the store that copies
them is wolf-lang#385's, ruled option 3 (s167, unreleased): `push`
copies a non-`Copy` element by default, deeply on the native tiers
(`[mem.tier0.move.3]`, wolf-lang#384) — a scalar costs nothing, a
`str` shares its bytes, a `List` element copies its buffer. No `copy`
is spelled here, because that default is already it.

```wolf-doc-example
var xs = List[str]()
list.push(mut xs, "a")
list.push(mut xs, "b")
let pairs = list.enumerate(xs)
let second = pairs[1]
second.0 == 1
second.1 == "b"
```
items.summary: A new list pairing each element of `xs` with its index, in order: `(0, x0), (1, x1), …`.

doctests.code:

list.push(mut xs, "a")
list.push(mut xs, "b")
let pairs = list.enumerate(xs)
let second = pairs[1]
second.0 == 1
second.1 == "b"

items.name: extend
items.sig: fn extend[T](mut xs: prelude.List[T], other: prelude.List[T]) · regions (ρ1, ρ2) -> -
items.doc:
Appends every element of `other` to `xs`, in order. `other` is read,
not consumed — the caller keeps it. Total: no error row, no traps
beyond allocation.

```wolf-doc-example
var xs = List[int]()
var ys = List[int]()
list.push(mut xs, 1)
list.push(mut ys, 2)
list.extend(mut xs, ys)
list.len(xs) == 2
(list.last(xs) else 0) == 2
```
