items.name: filter
items.sig: fn filter[T](xs: prelude.List[T], keep: fn(T) -> bool) -> prelude.List[T] · regions (ρ1, -) -> ρ_caller
items.doc:
A new list holding the elements of `xs` for which `keep` holds, in
their original order; `xs` is read, not consumed. The in-place
sibling (`retain`) is not written: a returning `filter` is the
combinator, and a `mut` twin would be a second name for one walk.
Total: no error row, no traps beyond allocation.

`[type.comb.set]` (wolf-lang `4c046f15`): the method `xs.filter(keep)`
is this call (`[type.method.resolve]` step 2). Cost, as the clause
states it: one fresh `List[T]` of at most `xs.len` in the ambient
region, and `xs.len` calls of `keep`, plus one element copy per kept
element — `push`'s own, not one spelled here.

**Why no `copy` is written.** `xs` is a `read` parameter, so an
element moved out of it is LENT and may not escape this call
(`[mem.tier0.mode.read]`, wolf-lang#366, in 0.2.15) — and the kept
elements do escape, in the returned list. That clause says in its own
words that it does not reach the builtin store which keeps a `read`
argument inside its receiver; that is wolf-lang#385, **ruled option
3** (s167, unreleased): `push` COPIES a non-`Copy` element by
default, and `push(take v)` moves it. The default copy is exactly the
copy this function needs, so writing `copy x` here would buy a second
one. `push`'s copy is deep on the native tiers (`[mem.tier0.move.3]`,
wolf-lang#384): a `List` element copies its buffer, a `str` element
shares its immutable bytes, a scalar costs nothing. Nothing is lent
out of this module either way, at this pin or at the next.

```wolf-doc-example
var xs = List[int]()
list.push(mut xs, 1)
list.push(mut xs, 2)
list.push(mut xs, 3)
list.len(list.filter(xs, fn(v) v % 2 == 1)) == 2
(list.last(list.filter(xs, fn(v) v % 2 == 1)) else 0) == 3
```
items.summary: A new list holding the elements of `xs` for which `keep` holds, in their original order; `xs` is read, not consumed.

doctests.code:
var xs = List[int]()
list.push(mut xs, 1)
list.push(mut xs, 2)
list.push(mut xs, 3)
list.len(list.filter(xs, fn(v) v % 2 == 1)) == 2
(list.last(list.filter(xs, fn(v) v % 2 == 1)) else 0) == 3

items.name: fold
items.sig: fn fold[T, A](xs: prelude.List[T], init: A, step: fn(A, T) -> A) -> A · regions (ρ1, ρ2, -) -> ρ_caller
items.doc:
Combines every element of `xs` into one value, left to right:
`f(… f(f(init, x0), x1) …, xn)`. `init` is the answer for the empty
list. The accumulator's type `A` need not be the element's. Total:
no error row, no traps beyond whatever `step` traps.

`[type.comb.set]` (wolf-lang `4c046f15`): the method `xs.fold(init,
step)` is this call (`[type.method.resolve]` step 2). Cost, as the
clause states it: no allocation of its own, and `xs.len` calls of
`step`, left to right. The clause's `f64` sum is this function:
`xs.fold(0.0, fn(a, x) a + x)`.

```wolf-doc-example
var xs = List[int]()
list.push(mut xs, 1)
list.push(mut xs, 2)
list.push(mut xs, 3)
list.fold(xs, 0, fn(acc, v) acc + v) == 6
```
items.summary: Combines every element of `xs` into one value, left to right: `f(… f(f(init, x0), x1) …, xn)`.

list.push(mut xs, 2)
list.push(mut xs, 3)

items.name: get
items.sig: fn get[T](xs: prelude.List[T], i: int) -> T ! {none} · regions (ρ1, -) -> ρ_caller
items.doc:
The element at `i`, checked: `none` when `i` is negative or at least
`len(xs)` — the one checked-access spelling (§1: no `get_` prefix, no
sentinel). No traps; the unchecked spelling is the language's `xs[i]`,
which traps `bounds`.

```wolf-doc-example
var xs = List[int]()
list.push(mut xs, 9)
(list.get(xs, 0) else 0 - 1) == 9
(list.get(xs, 4) else 0 - 1) == 0 - 1
(list.get(xs, 0 - 1) else 0 - 1) == 0 - 1
```
items.summary: The element at `i`, checked: `none` when `i` is negative or at least `len(xs)` — the one checked-access spelling (§1: no `get_` prefix, no sentinel).

doctests.code:

items.name: index_where
items.sig: fn index_where[T](xs: prelude.List[T], pred: fn(T) -> bool) -> int ! {none} · regions (ρ1, -) -> -
items.doc:
The index of the FIRST element satisfying `pred`; `none` when none
does. The index answers "where", `find_where` answers "what" — two
fns because a `T` is not an `int` and a sentinel index is §1's
forbidden shape.
items.summary: The index of the FIRST element satisfying `pred`; `none` when none does.

items.name: insert
items.sig: fn insert[T](mut xs: prelude.List[T], i: int, v: T) · regions (ρ1, -, ρ2) -> -
items.doc:
Inserts `v` at `i`, shifting the elements from `i` onward one place
to the right; `i == len(xs)` appends. Traps `bounds` when `i` is
negative or greater than `len(xs)`.

```wolf-doc-example
var xs = List[int]()
list.push(mut xs, 1)
list.push(mut xs, 3)
list.insert(mut xs, 1, 2)
(list.get(xs, 1) else 0) == 2
list.len(xs) == 3
```
items.summary: Inserts `v` at `i`, shifting the elements from `i` onward one place to the right; `i == len(xs)` appends.

items.sig: fn len[T](xs: prelude.List[T]) -> int · regions (ρ1) -> -


items.name: map
items.sig: fn map[T, U](xs: prelude.List[T], f: fn(T) -> U) -> prelude.List[U] · regions (ρ1, -) -> ρ_caller
items.doc:
A new list holding `f(x)` for every `x` in `xs`, in order; `xs` is
read, not consumed. The empty list maps to the empty list. Total: no
error row, no traps beyond allocation and whatever `f` traps.

`[type.comb.set]` (wolf-lang `4c046f15`): the method `xs.map(f)` is
this call (`[type.method.resolve]` step 2), and eager
(`[type.comb.eager]`). Cost, as the clause states it: one fresh
`List[U]` of `xs.len` in the ambient region, and `xs.len` calls of
`f`. A fallible `f` is `par`'s alone (`[conc.task.par]`).

**The one element here that this call OWNS, and the spelling it is
owed.** What this list holds is `f`'s own return value, not an
element moved out of `xs`, so nothing lent escapes
(`[mem.tier0.mode.read]`, wolf-lang#366); `x` is only LENT to `f` for
the call, which is what a `read` parameter is for, and an `f` that
hands its own argument back is the caller's site, not this one.
Because `f(x)` is a temporary this activation owns, the right
spelling under wolf-lang#385 (ruled option 3, s167, unreleased) is
`(mut out).push(take f(x))`, which MOVES it where the default copies.
It is not written yet because it does not exist yet: at wolf 0.2.14
both compiler rungs answer `E1007 — `push` takes `value` as plain
`read`, no mode is written for it` (measured, F-0136), and that is a
static refusal of this whole module, so every `std.list` row on both
rungs would pay for it. It lands with the pin that carries s167, and
the cost line above changes with it.

```wolf-doc-example
var xs = List[int]()
list.push(mut xs, 1)
list.push(mut xs, 2)
let ys = list.map(xs, fn(v) v * 10)
list.len(ys) == 2
(list.last(ys) else 0) == 20
```
items.summary: A new list holding `f(x)` for every `x` in `xs`, in order; `xs` is read, not consumed.

items.name: max_by
items.sig: fn max_by[T](xs: prelude.List[T], better: fn(T, T) -> bool) -> T ! {none} · regions (ρ1, -) -> ρ_caller
items.doc:
`min_by` under the flipped relation, named for the call sites that
read better with it. `max_by(xs, gt)` == `min_by(xs, gt)` when `gt`

caller writes a lambdaless flip by hand.

items.name: sort_by
items.sig: fn sort_by[T](mut xs: prelude.List[T], less: fn(T, T) -> bool) · regions (ρ1, -) -> -
items.doc:
Sorts `xs` in place, stably, under `less`, where `less(a, b)` reads
"`a` goes before `b`". Equal elements (neither goes before the other)
keep their input order: the merge takes from the right run only when
`less(right, left)` holds. `less` must be a strict weak order or the
result is merely a permutation; std cannot check that and does not
pretend to. Total: no error row, no traps beyond allocation and
whatever `less` traps. `std.sort`'s bottom-up merge, line for line.
The result satisfies `is_sorted_by(xs, fn(a, b) !less(b, a))`.

`[type.comb.set]` (wolf-lang `4c046f15`): the method
`(mut xs).sort_by(less)` is this call, its receiver's `mut` spelled
(`[type.method.resolve]`, X1). Cost, as the clause states it: stable,
O(n log n) calls of `less`, O(n) scratch in the ambient region, and
no `copy` at all: the receiver is `mut`, not `read`, so no element
here is lent and the sorted elements go back to the caller's own list
(`[mem.tier0.mode.read]`, wolf-lang#366). The returning twin
`sorted_by` pays the copies instead, because its receiver is `read`.

**Why the relation is `bool` and why `std.sort` keeps its own.** The
clause rules it: `std.sort.sort_by` takes a `cmp.Ordering`, and at
wolf 0.2.14 / lupin 0.1.36 it runs on no lane (re-measured for this
function: lupin declines the enum's dynamics at resolve, the checked
machine declines `std.cmp`'s module items, the native rung finds
`.is_lt()` untyped; F-0029). `std.sort`'s `Ordering` pair keeps its
qualified spelling; the method is this one. Same mode, same
stability, same algorithm; the comparator's type is the one
difference, and it is stated on both.

Call shape (a prose example, witnessed by `tests/list/sort_by_tier.lu`
on all three lanes): `fn shorter(a: str, b: str) -> bool { a.len <
b.len }` … then `list.sort_by(mut words, shorter)`. Not fenced: the
call is a statement, and §4's extractor reads a line holding the
relation's `<` as an assertion. `sorted_by`'s example is fenced and
shows the same order. Do not name a top-level fn `less` in a program
that passes a different relation: the checked machine calls it
instead of the argument (F-0134, wolf-lang#400).
items.summary: Sorts `xs` in place, stably, under `less`, where `less(a, b)` reads "`a` goes before `b`".

items.name: sorted
items.sig: fn sorted[T: std.cmp.Ord](xs: prelude.List[T]) -> prelude.List[T] · regions (ρ1) -> ρ_caller
items.doc:
A fresh list holding `xs`'s elements in `T`'s own ascending order,
stably, with `xs` untouched. `T: cmp.Ord` is a total order by its own
law, so this needs no relation from the caller. Total: no error row,
no traps beyond allocation.

`[type.comb.set]` (wolf-lang `4c046f15`): the method `xs.sorted()` is
this call. Cost, as the clause states it: `sorted_by` with `<`
(`[type.trait.op]`) — O(n log n) comparisons, O(n) scratch, plus
`push`'s own copy per element (#385 option 3, as the other
combinators).

**Its lanes, and the two rows behind them** (F-0135). It ships at
wolf-std `42d42b9` and not before: until sc49 rewrote `std.cmp`'s
`Ordering` impls without a product pattern, the `use std.cmp` above
made EVERY importer of this module `unsupported` on the native rung,
which is the "budget a module by its worst body" rule. The checked
machine still declines this one function — "trait dispatch on a
non-nominal receiver" at `a < b`, where `T` is bound through a list
read (wolf-lang#402) — so `tests/list/sorted_tier.lu` is
`unsupported` there and nothing else in the module pays for it.
Prose, not a fenced example, for that reason: §4 wants a lane that
refuses honestly, and lupin and native both run it —
`list.sorted(xs)` over `[3, 1, 2]` answers `1, 2, 3`.
items.summary: A fresh list holding `xs`'s elements in `T`'s own ascending order, stably, with `xs` untouched.

items.name: sorted_by
items.sig: fn sorted_by[T](xs: prelude.List[T], less: fn(T, T) -> bool) -> prelude.List[T] · regions (ρ1, -) -> ρ_caller
items.doc:
`sort_by`'s returning twin: a fresh list holding `xs`'s elements in
`less`'s order, stably, with `xs` untouched. `less` must be a strict
weak order or the result is merely a permutation. Total: no error
row, no traps beyond allocation and whatever `less` traps.

`[type.comb.set]` (wolf-lang `4c046f15`): the method
`xs.sorted_by(less)` is this call, the chain's sort (`corpus/
wordcount.lu`'s `sorted_by`). Cost, as the clause states it:
`sort_by` over a fresh copy, plus `push`'s own copy per element
building that copy — the elements escape in the returned list and
`xs` is a `read` parameter (`[mem.tier0.mode.read]`, wolf-lang#366),
and the store that copies them is wolf-lang#385's, ruled option 3
(s167, unreleased), deep on the native tiers
(`[mem.tier0.move.3]`, wolf-lang#384).
`std.sort.sorted_by` is the `Ordering` twin that runs on no lane
(F-0029) and keeps its qualified spelling.

```wolf-doc-example
list.push(mut xs, 1)
list.push(mut xs, 2)

(list.last(list.sorted_by(xs, fn(a, b) a < b)) else 0) == 3
(list.first(xs) else 0) == 3
```
items.summary: `sort_by`'s returning twin: a fresh list holding `xs`'s elements in `less`'s order, stably, with `xs` untouched.

items.doc:
The sum of `xs`; 0 for the empty list. Traps `overflow` the moment a
partial sum leaves `int` (checked arithmetic, X3), deliberately not a

this call on a `List[int]`, and on any other `List` it is E0403, not
a match. Cost, as the clause states it: none beyond checked addition
left to right (X3).

every importer of `std.cmp` is `unsupported` on the native rung (the
`search/*` rows carry exactly that), so the bound would cost every
`std.list` importer a lane; `std.ops` has no zero for `T` either. The
generic reduction is `fold`. `std.search.sum` stays: two modules may
share a function name (a program importing both links at this pin,
measured natively on `list.len` beside `bytes.len`), and this one
is the three-lane spelling.

items.name: zip
items.sig: fn zip[T, U](xs: prelude.List[T], ys: prelude.List[U]) -> prelude.List[(T, U)] · regions (ρ1, ρ2) -> ρ_caller
items.doc:
A new list pairing the elements of `xs` and `ys` position by
position: `(x0, y0), (x1, y1), …`, as long as the SHORTER of the two,
so the longer list's tail is dropped rather than trapped on. Both
operands are read, not consumed. Built through the private `fresh`
for the reason `enumerate` is (F-0133). Total: no error row, no traps
beyond allocation.

`[type.comb.set]` (wolf-lang `4c046f15`): the method `xs.zip(ys)` is
this call. Cost, as the clause states it: one fresh `List` of
`min(xs.len, ys.len)` pairs, plus `push`'s own copy of each pair —
BOTH lists are `read` parameters and both elements escape inside the
pairs (`[mem.tier0.mode.read]`, wolf-lang#366), and the copy that
makes that legal is `push`'s under wolf-lang#385, ruled option 3
(s167, unreleased), deep on the native tiers
(`[mem.tier0.move.3]`, wolf-lang#384). It stops at the shorter list
because a length mismatch is not an access out of range.

```wolf-doc-example
var names = List[str]()
list.push(mut names, "ada")
list.push(mut names, "grace")
var scores = List[int]()
list.push(mut scores, 91)
let rows = list.zip(names, scores)
list.len(rows) == 1
var total = 0
for (n, s) in rows { total = total + s + n.len }
total == 94
```
items.summary: A new list pairing the elements of `xs` and `ys` position by position: `(x0, y0), (x1, y1), …`, as long as the SHORTER of the two, so the longer list's tail is dropped rather than trapped on.

modules.doc:
std.map — the documented API surface of the prelude's `Map[K, V]`:
the keyed store the wordcount exemplar is written against. Stability
tier: core.

**WHAT IS THE LANGUAGE'S AND WHAT IS STD'S — RULED, and this header
stops being a filing.** F-0011 asked three questions when this module
was written (sc02) and s152 (`[type.map]`, `[type.map.key]`,
`[mem.map.absent]`; wolf-lang#11 item 4, #154) answers two of them
and leaves the third exactly as it was:

- **The key protocol: RULED, and there is no `Hash` half.** This
  header used to say "hashing lives inside the implementations and is
  unspecified … the `Hash` half is the filing's open question".
  `[type.map.key]` retires that sentence: `Map[K, V]` admits `str`,
  `int`, `char` and `bool` keys this edition — the four whose
  equality the LANGUAGE defines — and `[K: Eq]` is satisfied by the
  four through `std.cmp`'s ordinary impls. So the bound the five
  functions below already carried is not "the honest half" of a
  protocol; it is the whole of it. A struct key is E0418 and waits on
  derived equality, which is named upstream and unruled. `impl Eq for
  char` landed in `std.cmp` at sc44 for this clause: the ruling names
  four keys and that module shipped three impls.
- **`tally`: RULED, and it is std's.** The filed question was "is
  absent-key-defaulting a language rule or a std function?" and it
  closes the way the filing recommended. The LANGUAGE rules the
  absence — `m[k]` is `V ! {none}`, never `()`; `m[k] = v` inserts;
  `m[k] op= v` is E0417, whose note names `map.tally(mut m, k)` BY
  NAME — and STD owns the defaulting. `tally`'s body below is the
  clause's own spelling, unchanged since sc02 and now ruled rather
  than proposed.
- **Iteration order: unchanged, and deliberately.** `keys`, `values`
  and `pairs` promise the SAME order as each other for an unmodified
  map, and nothing more. Both machines answer insertion order at
  these pins and neither promise is made here.

`Map` itself stays the language's. The sc02 recommendation — that it
become a std-defined generic type — is answered in the other
direction and the answer is better than the recommendation: `Map` is
`TyKind::Map` in the compiler, a `wolf_rt::map` seam in the native
runtime and a served type in the checked machine, so it is a language
type with a spec clause instead of scaffolding with a deadline. This
module is the API surface over it, which is what §8's container rule
has said all along.

**LEDGER REALITY at the sc44 pins, measured rather than carried
forward.** The old paragraph said every function here is
`unsupported` under wolfc because `Map` is not typed there — "the
whole module is, honestly, freight". That is over. What replaced it
is not uniform and the differences are the point:

- The compiler's two rungs TYPE this module now, which means every
  body in it was read by the mem tier for the first time at this pin.
  One refusal fell out of that first reading and it is recorded at
  `set` below.
- The `[K: Eq]` five (`get`, `get_or`, `has`, `remove`, `tally`)
  EXECUTE on the checked tier AND on lupin, as of sc46. They were
  `unsupported` on the reference machine for one release, and the
  reason was never F-0002's old blanket claim: dispatch through a
  trait declared in the ENTRY FILE ran on all three machines while
  dispatch through an IMPORTED module's trait was `unsupported: `Eq`
  is a trait; traits, enums and type-level items have no dynamic
  semantics here`. Measured at sc44 with a twelve-line reduction,
  filed as wolf-interp#96, and CLOSED in is46 — so F-0002's last
  quarter goes with it. The three `[K: Eq]` rows flip
  `unsupported` -> `run` on lupin in this sprint's ledger commit.
- So the five are FENCED blocks again, which is what sc44 promised
  would happen "on the wolf-interp release that closes it, and
  nothing else has to change for that to happen" — nothing else did.
  Five examples, all five at `exit(0)` on the reference machine.
- The native rung refuses this module for a reason that is
  `std.cmp`'s and not `std.map`'s: `impl Eq for Ordering`'s
  `match (self, other)` is `unsupported — an enum or row test inside
  a product pattern (deep trees, c06)`. Every importer of `std.cmp`
  pays it; it is honest and it is older than this sprint.

Absence is spelled `none`, the convention's own spelling — F-0003 is
dead (sc05 pins, renamed at sc06) and nothing here waits on it.

items.sig: fn remove[K: std.cmp.Eq, V](mut m: prelude.Map[K, V], k: K) -> V ! {none} · regions (ρ1, ρ2) -> ρ_caller

when the key was absent. No traps.

wolf-lang#11, landed as wolf-lang#344), whose semantics are therefore
this function's contract. The erase happens in place. The survivors
keep their order, and a miss leaves the map unchanged. Its cost is the
clause's: one scan to the key and a shift of the entries after it,
with nothing allocated and nothing freed. Until sc52 this body rebuilt
the whole map through `pairs()`, about N^2 entry copies to empty an
N-entry map one key at a time. That ran past lupin's and the checked
tier's step budgets at 3000 keys (`tests/map/remove_many.lu`), and
the language had shipped the erase a release earlier (B117).
The `[K: cmp.Eq]` bound stays, because it is the module's key
protocol (`[type.map.key]`) and removing it would change the signature.
The body no longer calls it.

region — parameter regions are independent by default" — which took
the WHOLE module down on both rungs, not just this function.
`copy` is the fix-it the diagnostic itself suggests and it is in the
grammar now; the value is copied into the container's region, which
for the four key types and every `V` this edition admits is what a
caller means by `set`.

The asymmetry behind it is filed upstream: `(mut xs).push(v)` under

modules.doc:
std.range — operations over the language's `a..b`. Stability tier:
core.

**Four functions, all O(1), on the two accessors `[type.range]` gave
the type at wolf 0.2.14 (s158, wolf-lang#24; F-0030 CLOSED).** A
`range[int]` is a nameable type with `start` and `end` as properties,
and `end` is EXCLUSIVE, always: `a..=b` normalizes at construction to
`end = b + 1` under `[mem.iter.range]`'s checked arithmetic, so
`(2..=7).end` is 8 and `r.end - r.start` is the count for both
spellings (`[type.range.accessor]`). That one exclusive `end` is what
makes `contains`, `len` and `clamp_to` writable at all. sc04 reviewed
their signatures and F-0030 recorded them as unwritable for eleven
sprints, because the only spelling was iteration: O(len) for an O(1)
question, and a hang rather than an answer on
`0..9223372036854775807`. `is_empty` shipped alone, on the one fact
iteration can decide in O(1), and is now the same comparison as the
other three.

**A reversed range is a legal, empty value.** `7..3` iterates zero
times — `[mem.iter.range]` steps ascending while `< end` — so
`is_empty(7..3)` is true, and its raw `end - start` is **-4**,
measured at wolf 0.2.14 on both rungs. `len` therefore answers the
COUNT of values a `for` would yield, which is 0 there, and not the
signed difference wolf-std#30 spelled: a function named `len` that
answers a negative number is the wrong-on-legal-input shape sc03's
refusal-over-approximation rule (§9) does not ship. `clamp_to` on an
empty range has no member to answer with and raises `none` (§2:
absence is a row tag, never a sentinel), a row the reviewed signature
did not carry; returning `start` — a number the range does not
contain — would be the same wrong answer under a different name.

**Lane words, named.** Both compiler rungs run every row here at
0.2.14. The reference machine (lupin 0.1.36) conforms to `a7f517e` =
v0.2.12 and has not mirrored `[type.range.accessor]`: `r.start` and
`r.end` are declined BY NAME at resolve there — "a range has no
member `start`", F-0030's sentence, a whole-program `unsupported`
and never a diagnostic — so every test in `tests/range/` is
`unsupported` on lupin, `is_empty`'s included (it ran there while
its body was a loop). The examples below are FENCED, under the
extractor's `mirror-lag` word (`LUPIN_MIRROR_LAG`, wolf-std#37, sc49):
both compiler rungs must run each block to `exit(0)`, and the
reference lane must decline it with exactly that sentence. They were
prose at sc48 because `doc-examples` accepted a lupin `unsupported`
only for capability modules, and a fence would have been a red. The
release that mirrors the clause reds the five lupin test rows
(deeper than the ledger) AND these four blocks on the same day, and
the entry leaves in the commit that flips them.

**A fifth function, `collect`, is `[type.comb.set]`'s** (sc50, wolf-lang
`4c046f15`): the one combinator whose receiver is a range, and the
one here that reads no accessor. It walks `for x in r`, so lupin
0.1.36, which resolves lazily, runs it over `range[int]` and
declines `range[char]` itself ("a range needs integer endpoints").
Its int example is fenced for that reason.

`rev()` and `step_by()` remain BLOCKED on the iterator combinator
surface (F-0008's successor); the combinator that truncates a sequence
is named `limit(n)`, never `take(n)` — `take` is the ownership mode
that CONSUMES its operand, and a combinator that does not consume
would be a false friend at the centre of the ownership story
(wolf-lang#16, API-CONVENTIONS §10).

items.name: clamp_to
items.sig: fn clamp_to(r: prelude.range[int], x: int) -> int ! {none} · regions (ρ1, -) -> -
items.doc:
The value of `r` nearest to `x`: `x` itself when `r` contains it,
`r.start` when `x` lies below, and `r.end - 1` — the last value
yielded — when `x` is at or above `end`. Rows: `none` when `r` is
empty, because an empty range has no member to answer with (§2).
Never traps: `r.end - 1` is computed only under `r.start < r.end`,
so it cannot underflow.

An empty range answers with the row, handled here with `else`:

```wolf-doc-example
(range.clamp_to(2..7, 4) else 0 - 1) == 4
(range.clamp_to(2..7, 9) else 0 - 1) == 6
(range.clamp_to(2..7, 0 - 3) else 0 - 1) == 2
(range.clamp_to(5..5, 1) else 0 - 1) == 0 - 1
```
items.summary: The value of `r` nearest to `x`: `x` itself when `r` contains it, `r.start` when `x` lies below, and `r.end - 1` — the last value yielded — when `x` is at or above `end`.

doctests.code:
(range.clamp_to(2..7, 4) else 0 - 1) == 4
(range.clamp_to(2..7, 9) else 0 - 1) == 6
(range.clamp_to(2..7, 0 - 3) else 0 - 1) == 2
(range.clamp_to(5..5, 1) else 0 - 1) == 0 - 1

items.name: collect
items.sig: fn collect[T](r: prelude.range[T]) -> prelude.List[T] · regions (ρ1) -> ρ_caller
items.doc:
A fresh list holding every value `r` yields, in iteration order: the
values a `for x in r` would see. `2..5` collects `2, 3, 4`; an empty
or reversed range collects the empty list. One generic function for
both element types the clause names (`range[int]`, `range[char]`),
because wolf has no overloading and a `range[int]` signature refuses
a char range with `E0401` (measured). Total: no error row; traps as
the range's `for` does (`[mem.iter.range]`), and allocation. A
`0..9223372036854775807` collect is a list of that length, which no
host has, so no test here builds one.

`[type.comb.set]` (wolf-lang `4c046f15`): the method `r.collect()`
is this call (`std.range` is `range`'s home module,
`[type.method.home]`). Cost, as the clause states it: one fresh
`List` of the range's length, plus `push`'s own copy per value.

`r` is a `read` parameter and the values escape in the returned list
(`[mem.tier0.mode.read]`, wolf-lang#366, in 0.2.15), and that clause
counts a TYPE PARAMETER as able to reach shared storage always,
"because a generic body is checked once for every instantiation" — so
`T` is in scope for the rule even though the two element types a
range can have are scalars. No `copy` is spelled: the store is
`push`'s, wolf-lang#385 ruled option 3 (s167, unreleased) copies a
non-`Copy` element by default, and a value that reaches no heap
storage is its own copy, so this costs nothing at run time either way
(`[mem.tier0.move.3]`, wolf-lang#384). `take` is not the spelling
here: a value moved out of a `read` parameter is LENT, and a `take`
of a lent binding is E1014 by the same clause.

```wolf-doc-example
range.collect(2..5).len == 3
range.collect(2..5)[0] == 2
range.collect(1..=3)[2] == 3
range.collect(7..3).len == 0
```
items.summary: A fresh list holding every value `r` yields, in iteration order: the values a `for x in r` would see.

doctests.code:
range.collect(2..5).len == 3
range.collect(2..5)[0] == 2
range.collect(1..=3)[2] == 3
range.collect(7..3).len == 0

items.name: contains
items.sig: fn contains(r: prelude.range[int], x: int) -> bool · regions (ρ1, -) -> -
items.doc:
True when `x` is a value `r` yields: `r.start <= x && x < r.end`,
the spelling `[type.range.accessor]` gives. O(1) on every input,
`0..9223372036854775807` included — the range this function refused
to be written over by iteration. An empty range contains nothing.
Total: no error row, no traps.

`end` is exclusive, so `7` is outside `2..7` and inside `2..=7`:

```wolf-doc-example
range.contains(2..7, 2) == true
range.contains(2..7, 7) == false
range.contains(2..=7, 7) == true
```
items.summary: True when `x` is a value `r` yields: `r.start <= x && x < r.end`, the spelling `[type.range.accessor]` gives.

doctests.code:
range.contains(2..7, 2) == true
range.contains(2..7, 7) == false
range.contains(2..=7, 7) == true

items.name: is_empty
items.sig: fn is_empty(r: prelude.range[int]) -> bool · regions (ρ1) -> -
items.doc:
True when `r` yields no values — `5..5` and `7..3` are empty, `2..7`
is not. One comparison, `r.start >= r.end`; the body before 0.2.14
asked the iterator the same question (`for _ in r { return false }`),
which was O(1) too and is why this function shipped eleven sprints
before the other three. Total: no error row, no traps.

```wolf-doc-example
range.is_empty(5..5) == true
range.is_empty(7..3) == true
range.is_empty(2..7) == false
```
items.summary: True when `r` yields no values — `5..5` and `7..3` are empty, `2..7` is not.

doctests.code:
range.is_empty(5..5) == true
range.is_empty(7..3) == true
range.is_empty(2..7) == false

items.name: len
items.sig: fn len(r: prelude.range[int]) -> int · regions (ρ1) -> -
items.doc:
The number of values `r` yields: `r.end - r.start` when `r` is
non-empty, `0` when it is not — `len(7..3)` is 0 where the raw
difference is -4 (module header), and `len(a..=b)` is `b - a + 1`
because `end` normalized to `b + 1` at construction. No error row.
Traps `overflow` (checked arithmetic, X3) when the count does not fit
an `int`, which is exactly a range spanning more than half the
integer line — `(0 - 9223372036854775807 - 1)..9223372036854775807`
yields 2^64 - 1 values and there is no `int` to say so;
`tests/range/len_overflow_trap.lu` pins the kind.

```wolf-doc-example
range.len(2..7) == 5
range.len(2..=7) == 6
range.len(5..5) == 0
range.len(7..3) == 0
```

range.len(7..3) == 0

modules.doc:
std.strbuf — the one string builder (D24). Stability tier: core.

**What is the language's and what is std's.** Nothing here is the
language's yet: `str` is the language's immutable UTF-8 slice, and D24
promises `strbuf` as an owned, growable, SSO-backed builder that
auto-borrows to `str` — compiler-side plumbing (s37 §3) that does not
exist at this pin. This module is the API surface that plumbing will
back, written today over the one thing that does exist: a `str` field
rebuilt by interpolation.

THE BACKING IS AN INTERIM, and it is a performance interim, not a
semantic one. `push_str` allocates a fresh `str` and copies both sides,
so appending n times over a buffer of length m is O(n·m) where the SSO
builder is amortized O(n+m). Every function's meaning is final; the
complexity notes say "the SSO backing will make this O(1) amortized"
wherever that is the only difference. No caller has to change when the
backing lands (F-0019), and this file is where the layout note for
s41/s43's ABI document will hang.

`StrBuf` is CapCase per API-CONVENTIONS §1 even though the sprint
contract writes the constructor as `strbuf()`: a callable type name is
s37's builtin spelling, and `strbuf.new()` is the module spelling
available today. That delta is recorded in the campaign closeout.

TWO OF THE ELEVEN ARE NOT HERE, each for a stated reason — and
`push(c: char)` LEFT this list at sc24: D58 ruled the type
(`[type.char]`, the sc24 data pin) and the sc24 wolf pair executes
it, so the one-line body (`{c}` interpolation, which prints THE
CHARACTER per `[type.char.interp]`) is code below — on every
executing lane as of sc25: lupin 0.1.15 (is26, the scalar release)
runs `char`, and the row that sc24 ledgered by lane flipped at that
release as promised. The sc24 history stays worth a sentence: the
sprint's first wolf acquisition (@ e7abf03) was pre-s121 and refused
the type — the mid-sprint re-acquisition is what made this writable,
and every sentence here was re-measured against the binary pinned.

- `strbuf.in(r)` — the region-explicit constructor (API-CONVENTIONS §5,
  the s37 `.in(r)` pattern). Placement syntax over a std type is
  compiler plumbing this pin does not have; the ambient-region
  constructor below is D10's default and needs no annotation.
  **RE-PROBED rather than argued at the sc32 pin v0.2.2/8cda3aa
  (2026-09-02), because for the first time in this residue's life
  the span MOVED regions for real** — s131 and s132 landed the byte
  ledger, the creation-time cap and D68's contained fault
  whole-pipe, so "regions did not change" stopped being a sentence a
  reader should take on trust. The probe is the placement syntax
  itself, both shapes: `List[int].in(r)` is `unsupported — a
  std/prelude stub without a signature` at resolve on both wolf
  rungs AND refused by lupin, and `Buf.in(r) { … }` over a plain
  struct is `fail(E0201)` at PARSE on all three — the form does not
  exist in the grammar, which is the honest state of a surface
  nobody has built. s131/s132 gave regions an ACCOUNTING surface and
  a BUDGET; they gave them no placement plumbing, and the two are
  different work. `std.mem.budget` is what this repo consumed from
  that span instead.
- `reserve(n)` — API-CONVENTIONS §8's rule ("no capacity API without a
  capacity") applies verbatim: a `str`-backed buffer has no capacity to
  reserve, and a documented no-op would be a lie. It lands with the SSO
  backing that gives it meaning. UNMOVED at the sc32 pin
  (2026-09-02): there is no capacity or string-backing commit
  anywhere in `75fd2d0..8cda3aa` or `0.1.20..0.1.22`. And the
  question this line carried forward from sc31 is now ANSWERED
  rather than deferred — the region accounting surface wolf-lang#187
  asked for landed in this span (both halves: `region_bytes`/
  `live_region_bytes` from s131, the `cap:` budget and its contained
  `fault(kind)` from s132/D68), it was consumed at sc32, and it
  lives in `std.mem.budget`. It bought this module nothing, which is
  the honest outcome: a ledger tells you what a buffer COST and a
  cap tells you when to stop, and neither is a capacity you can
  reserve.

Absence is spelled `none` where it appears, which is the convention's
own spelling: F-0003 died at the sc05 pins and the rename landed
tree-wide at sc06, so nothing here is waiting on it.

```wolf-doc-example
strbuf.push_str(mut b, "wolf")
strbuf.clear(mut b)
```

items.name: insert
items.sig: fn insert(mut b: self.StrBuf, off: int, s: str) · regions (ρ1, -, -) -> -
items.doc:
Inserts `s` at byte offset `off`, shifting everything at or after `off`
to the right. `off == len(b)` appends; `off == 0` prepends.

Traps `bounds` (`[conf.trap.set]`) when `off` is out of range or falls
inside a code point — the language's own checked slicing (D25), raised
exactly where a caller would see it. That is the "checked boundary" the
contract asks for; the recoverable form — an `insert` that raises
rather than traps — is writable over `str.get` as of s37 (sc09) and is
a `std.strbuf` sprint's to add, under its own name, beside this one.

```wolf-doc-example
var b = strbuf.new()
strbuf.push_str(mut b, "wolf")
strbuf.insert(mut b, 0, "the ")
strbuf.to_str(b) == "the wolf"
```

items.name: push
items.sig: fn push(mut b: self.StrBuf, c: char) · regions (ρ1, -) -> -
items.doc:
Appends one code point — the sc03 contract's `push(c)`, code at last
(sc24), over D58's `char` (`[type.char]`: a Unicode scalar value,
ordered, NOT an integer). The body is `b.s += c`, which
`[type.str.concat]` rules to append THE CHARACTER — so the appended
bytes are exactly `c`'s UTF-8 encoding, 1 to 4 of them, and the
buffer's UTF-8 validity is preserved by construction: no `int` ever
touches this path, and a non-scalar cannot exist as a `char` at all
(the D56 cast already trapped it). O(len(b)) with the interim
backing, amortized O(1) once the SSO builder lands. Total: no error
row, no traps beyond allocation.

**It was an interpolation hole until sc43** — `b.s = "{b.s}{c}"` —
and the hole existed for exactly one reason: `+` refused a `char`,
so the only way to put one on the end of a `str` was to render it
into a new string. wolf-lang#278 admitted a `char` on either side of
`+` and as the value of `+=` at v0.2.9, and lupin 0.1.31 mirrored it
(is43, wolf-interp#78). The two appenders are written in one idiom
now — this line and `push_str`'s are the same line with a different
operand type — and `[type.char.interp]` is no longer what carries
the character across; `[type.str.concat]` is.

LANES: every executing lane runs this as of the sc25 pins — both
wolf rungs since s121, lupin since 0.1.15 (is26, the scalar
release; sc24's one-sprint `unsupported` there closed on it). The
example keeps its `"é🐺".chars()` spelling because the walk is the
natural producer here, not as the lex-dodge it was under 0.1.14.

```wolf-doc-example
var b = strbuf.new()
for c in "é🐺".chars() { strbuf.push(mut b, c) }
strbuf.to_str(b) == "é🐺"
strbuf.len(b) == 6
```
items.summary: Appends one code point — the sc03 contract's `push(c)`, code at last (sc24), over D58's `char` (`[type.char]`: a Unicode scalar value, ordered, NOT an integer).

items.name: push_str
items.sig: fn push_str(mut b: self.StrBuf, s: str) · regions (ρ1, -) -> -
items.doc:
Appends `s` to the end of the buffer. O(len(b) + len(s)) with the
interim backing, amortized O(len(s)) once the SSO builder lands. Total:
no error row, no traps beyond allocation.

The `+=` spelling the sprint contract mentions — `b += s` on the
BUFFER — is not available: the operator-to-method bridge is F-0004's
open question, and wolf has no operator overloading, so a `StrBuf`
cannot be the left side of one. `push_str` is the one spelling std
writes. (The sentence that stood here until sc43 went on to say `+`
on `str` "runs in lupin and is E0409 in wolfc". That was true when it
was written and stopped being true at D62, which this very body
adopted: `b.s += s` is a `str` `+=` on all three lanes, and sc43's
`push` is now its `char` twin one function down.)

```wolf-doc-example
var b = strbuf.new()
strbuf.push_str(mut b, "wolf")
strbuf.push_str(mut b, "-lang")
strbuf.to_str(b) == "wolf-lang"
```
items.summary: Appends `s` to the end of the buffer.

items.name: remove
items.sig: fn remove(mut b: self.StrBuf, from: int, to: int) · regions (ρ1, -, -) -> -
items.doc:
Removes the bytes in `[from, to)`, closing the gap. Empty when
`from == to`.

Traps `bounds` when the range is out of order, out of range, or splits
a code point (D25, as `insert`). The contract writes this as
`remove(a..b)`; a range is not a value that can cross a function
boundary at this pin (`fn f(r: Range)` is E0301 in wolfc), so the two
offsets are spelled as two parameters — the same interim `str.get`
carries, flipping together with it.

```wolf-doc-example
var b = strbuf.new()
strbuf.push_str(mut b, "the wolf")
strbuf.remove(mut b, 0, 4)
strbuf.to_str(b) == "wolf"
```

items.name: to_str
items.sig: fn to_str(b: self.StrBuf) -> str · regions (ρ1) -> -
items.doc:
The buffer's contents as a `str`. A borrow of the buffer's bytes under
D24's auto-borrow story — `as_`/bare-noun territory in
API-CONVENTIONS §1 rather than an allocating `to_`. The name is the
contract's; with the interim backing the value shares the field's
buffer, which is the borrow the final type promises. Total: no error
row, no traps.

```wolf-doc-example
var b = strbuf.new()
strbuf.push_str(mut b, "wolf")
strbuf.to_str(b) == "wolf"
```

items.name: truncate
items.sig: fn truncate(mut b: self.StrBuf, n: int) · regions (ρ1, -) -> -
items.doc:
Shortens the buffer to `n` bytes, dropping everything after. Keeps the
buffer usable and is a no-op when `n == len(b)`.

Traps `bounds` when `n` exceeds the length or splits a code point (D25)
— truncation is exactly a checked slice.

```wolf-doc-example
var b = strbuf.new()
strbuf.push_str(mut b, "wolf-lang")
strbuf.truncate(mut b, 4)
strbuf.to_str(b) == "wolf"
```
